chapters.title: Preface
paragraphs: People have rightly called Shakespeare’s writings “the richest, the purest, the fairest, that genius uninspired ever penned.”

Shakespeare taught by giving delight. Setting science aside, his plays alone hold more real wisdom than all the rest of English learning put together. He teaches everything good: pity, generosity, true courage, love. His bright wit is cut up “into little stars.” His solid stores of knowledge are handed out in small pieces and proverbs, and spread that way, they light up nearly every corner of the English-speaking world today and enrich every cottage in it. His generosity is like the sea, which is felt everywhere even when no one thanks it. As his friend Ben Jonson wrote of him, “He was not of an age but for all time.” He always stayed on the high road of human life, the road everyone travels, and never wandered down side paths of feeling and sentiment. In the people he created there are no moral highwaymen, no sentimental thieves, no charming villains, no gracious and elegant adventuresses. There are no delicate tangles of plot in which the coarsest images are slipped into the mind behind the pleasing surface of fine style and feeling. He never flattered a bad passion, never dressed up a vice as a virtue, and never made light of any just and generous principle. He makes us laugh at foolishness and shudder at crime, and yet he leaves us still loving our fellow human beings and still respecting ourselves.

Shakespeare knew every beautiful form and image. He knew all that is sweet or grand in the plain sights of nature, and he shared that lasting love of flowers and fragrance, of dew and clear water, of soft breezes and sounds, of bright skies, lonely woods and moonlit arbors, which are the raw materials of poetry. He also had a fine sense of how these things connect, in ways hard to put into words, with the feelings of the mind, which is the very essence and living soul of poetry. Even in the busiest and most tragic of his scenes, that sense falls like patches of sunshine on rocks and ruins. It stands out against everything harsh or ugly and reminds us that purer and brighter things exist.

Given all this, is it any wonder that, after the Bible, Shakespeare’s works are valued more highly than any other classics of English literature? An American author says, “Artists, poets and novelists have drawn so widely on Shakespeare’s characters, and these characters are so woven into the whole body of English literature, that not knowing the plots of these plays is often embarrassing.”
But Shakespeare wrote for grown men and women, in words that young children cannot understand.

That is why this book exists. The author of these Beautiful Stories from Shakespeare set out to retell the entertaining stories found in Shakespeare’s plays, in a form so simple that children can understand and enjoy them.

So that the youngest readers will not trip over any unfamiliar names in the stories, the editor has also put a Pronouncing Vocabulary of Difficult Names into the book. Added to this is a collection of Shakespearean Quotations, arranged in alphabetical order, which show the wisdom and genius of the greatest playwright in the world.
E. T. R.

chapters.title: A Brief Life of Shakespeare
paragraphs: The register of baptisms at the parish church of Stratford-upon-Avon, a market town in Warwickshire, England, records an entry dated April 26, 1564: the baptism of William, son of John Shakspeare. The entry is written in Latin: “Gulielmus filius Johannis Shakspeare.”
People usually assume that William Shakespeare was born three days before he was baptized, but there is certainly no evidence for that.

The family name was spelled in many ways, and the playwright himself did not always spell it the same way. The baptism record has “Shakspeare,” several genuine signatures of his read “Shakspere,” and the first edition of his works prints “Shakespeare.”

Halliwell tells us that members of the Shakespeare family wrote the name in at least thirty-four different ways. In the council book of the Stratford corporation, the name appears one hundred and sixty-six times while the playwright’s father sat on the town council, and it is spelled fourteen different ways. The modern “Shakespeare” is not one of them.

While he was an alderman of Stratford, Shakespeare’s father seems not to have been able to write his name. But in those days nine men out of ten simply made a mark as their signature, so this does not count much against him.

The traditions and other sources disagree about what Shakespeare’s father did for a living. He is called a butcher, a wool dealer and a glover. He may well have been all three, at once or at different times. Or, if none of these names fits him exactly, his trade may have been close enough to all of them to explain how the different traditions arose. Even before his marriage he owned land and farmed it himself. With his wife, Mary Arden, the daughter of a country gentleman, he received the estate of Asbies, which covered 56 acres. William was the third child. The two older ones were girls, and both probably died as babies. After William came three sons and a daughter. For at least ten or twelve years after Shakespeare’s birth, his father stayed comfortably well off. In 1568 he was high bailiff, the chief magistrate of Stratford, and he held the post of alderman for many years afterward, as he had for three years before. So it is natural to suppose that until he was ten, William Shakespeare received the best education Stratford could offer. The town’s free school was open to all boys. Like all the grammar schools of that time, it was run by university graduates, who were qualified to pass on the sound scholarship that was once England’s pride. There is no record that Shakespeare attended this school, but there can be no reasonable doubt that he was taught there, since his father could not have found him a better education anywhere. Anyone who studies Shakespeare’s works without being swayed by the old belief that his schooling was very narrow will find them full of signs that he must have been solidly grounded in the real learning taught in the grammar schools.

Stratford had local surroundings that could not fail to shape the young Shakespeare’s mind. Within reach of a curious boy were the fine old historic towns of Warwick and Coventry, the magnificent palace of Kenilworth and the great ruined monastery at Evesham. His own river Avon had many spots of unusual beauty, with quiet villages and lonely woods. Nor was Stratford cut off from the wider world, as many country towns are. It stood on a main road, and merchants selling every kind of goods came to its markets. The eyes of the poet and playwright must always have been open to what went on around him. Yet nothing is known for certain about Shakespeare from his birth until his marriage to Anne Hathaway in 1582. After that, we know only of the birth of three children, until we find him working as an actor in London around 1589.

We have no way of knowing how long acting remained Shakespeare’s only profession. But it is highly probable that soon after he reached London he began the work of adapting other writers’ plays, which is known to have started his career as a writer. Improving and changing older plays that no longer met the standards of the day was common even among the best playwrights of the time, and Shakespeare’s talents would quickly have shown him to be especially suited to it. When the changes to a play first written by someone else became very large, the adapting turned into real creation. A few of Shakespeare’s early works, which are known to be based on older plays, give us exactly this kind of example.

There is no need to praise the published works of the greatest playwright in the world here. Critics have said everything there is to say about them, and the finest minds of England, Germany and America have given their efforts to explaining their worth.

Shakespeare died at Stratford on April 23, 1616. His father had died before him, in 1602, and his mother in 1608. His wife outlived him until August 1623. His son Hamnet died in 1596 at the age of eleven. His two daughters outlived him. The elder, Susanna, had married a Stratford physician, Dr Hall, in 1607. Their only child, a daughter named Elizabeth, born in 1608, married first Thomas Nasbe and later Sir John Barnard, but had no children with either husband. Shakespeare’s younger daughter, Judith, married a Stratford gentleman named Thomas Quincy on February 10, 1616. They had three sons, but all of them died without children. So Shakespeare has no direct descendants.

Shakespeare’s fellow actors, fellow playwrights and others who knew him all said the same thing: they admired his genius, and they respected and loved the man. Ben Jonson said, “I love the man, and do honor his memory, on this side idolatry, as much as any. He was indeed honest, and of an open and free nature.” Shakespeare was buried two days after he died, on the north side of the chancel of Stratford church. Over his grave lies a flat stone with this inscription, said to have been written by Shakespeare himself:

Good friend, for Jesus’ sake, refrain
From digging the dust enclosed here.
Blessed be the man who spares these stones,
And cursed be he who moves my bones.

chapters.title: A Midsummer Night’s Dream
paragraphs: Hermia and Lysander were in love, but Hermia’s father wanted her to marry a different man, called Demetrius.

Now, in Athens, where they lived, there was a cruel law: any girl who refused to marry the man her father chose could be put to death. Hermia’s father was so furious at her refusal that he took her before the Duke of Athens and asked that she be killed if she still would not obey him. The Duke gave her four days to think it over. When that time was up, if she still refused to marry Demetrius, she would have to die.

Lysander was naturally almost out of his mind with grief. The best plan he could think of was for Hermia to run away to his aunt’s house, in a place beyond the reach of that cruel law. He would come to her there and marry her. But before she set out, Hermia told her friend Helena what she was going to do.

Helena had been Demetrius’s sweetheart long before anyone thought of his marrying Hermia. Like all jealous people, she was being very silly, because she could not see that it was not poor Hermia’s fault that Demetrius wanted to marry her instead of his own lady, Helena. Helena knew that if she told Demetrius that Hermia was going to the wood outside Athens, as she was, he would follow her. “And I can follow him, and at least I shall see him,” she said to herself. So she went to Demetrius and betrayed her friend’s secret.

The wood where Lysander was to meet Hermia, and where the other two had decided to follow them, was full of fairies, as most woods are, if you only have the eyes to see them. That night the King and Queen of the fairies, Oberon and Titania, were in the wood. Fairies are very wise people, but now and then they can be just as foolish as human beings. Oberon and Titania could have been as happy as the days were long, but they had thrown away all their joy in a silly quarrel. They could not meet without saying unpleasant things to each other, and they scolded each other so terribly that all their little fairy followers crept into acorn cups out of fear and hid there.

So instead of holding one happy court and dancing all night in the moonlight, as fairies usually do, the King and his attendants wandered through one part of the wood, while the Queen and hers held court in another. The cause of all this trouble was a little Indian boy whom Titania had taken in as one of her followers. Oberon wanted the child to follow him and become one of his fairy knights, but the Queen would not give him up.
That night, in a mossy glade lit by the moon, the King and Queen of the fairies met.
“A bad meeting by moonlight, proud Titania,” said the King.
“What, jealous, Oberon?” the Queen answered. “You spoil everything with your quarreling. Come, fairies, let’s leave him. I’m not friends with him anymore.”
“It’s up to you to end the quarrel,” said the King.
“Hand over that little Indian boy, and I’ll be your humble servant and admirer once more.”
“Forget it,” said the Queen. “You couldn’t buy that boy from me with your entire fairy kingdom. Come along, fairies.”
And she and her followers rode away down the moonbeams.
“Very well, go your way,” said Oberon. “But I’ll get even with you before you leave this wood.”

Then Oberon called for his favorite fairy, Puck. Puck was the spirit of mischief. He would slip into dairies and steal the cream, jump into the churn so the butter wouldn’t form, and turn the beer sour. He led people off their path on dark nights and then laughed at them. He pulled stools out from under people just as they were about to sit down, and tipped their hot ale over their chins just as they were about to drink.

“Now,” Oberon said to the little sprite, “bring me the flower called Love-in-idleness. If you put the juice of that little purple flower on the eyes of someone who is asleep, that person will fall in love, on waking, with the first thing they see. I will put some of its juice on my Titania’s eyes, and when she wakes she will love the first thing she sees, whether it is a lion, a bear, a wolf, a bull, a meddling monkey or a busy ape.”

While Puck was away, Demetrius came through the glade with poor Helena following him. She kept telling him how much she loved him and reminding him of all his promises, and he kept telling her that he did not and could not love her, and that his promises meant nothing. Oberon felt sorry for poor Helena. When Puck came back with the flower, Oberon ordered him to follow Demetrius and put some of the juice on his eyes, so that when he woke and saw Helena he would love her as much as she loved him. So Puck set off. As he wandered through the wood, he found Lysander instead of Demetrius, and put the juice on Lysander’s eyes. But when Lysander woke, the person he saw was not his own Hermia but Helena, who was walking through the wood in search of the cruel Demetrius. The moment he saw her he fell in love with her and abandoned his own lady, under the spell of the purple flower.

When Hermia woke up, Lysander was gone, and she wandered through the wood trying to find him. Puck returned and told Oberon what he had done. Oberon soon realized that Puck had made a mistake, so he went looking for Demetrius, and when he found him, he put some of the juice on his eyes. The first thing Demetrius saw when he woke was Helena, too. So now both Demetrius and Lysander were chasing her through the wood, and it was Hermia’s turn to chase her lover, just as Helena had done before. In the end, Helena and Hermia began to quarrel, and Demetrius and Lysander went off to fight. Oberon was very sorry to see his kind plan for helping these lovers turn out so badly. So he said to Puck—

“Those two young men are about to fight. Cover the night in thick, drooping fog and lead them astray, so that neither one can find the other. Once they are worn out, they will fall asleep. Then drop the juice of this other herb on Lysander’s eyes. It will give him back his old sight and his old love. Each man will then have the lady who loves him, and all four will believe it was nothing more than a Midsummer Night’s Dream. When that is done, everything will be well with them.”
So Puck went off and did as he was told. When the two young men had fallen asleep without ever meeting, Puck poured the juice on Lysander’s eyes and said:

“When you wake up,
You will take
True delight
In the sight
Of your former lady’s eye:
Jack gets Jill;
Nothing will go ill.”

Meanwhile Oberon found Titania asleep on a bank where wild thyme grew, along with oxlips, violets, woodbine, musk-roses, and eglantine. Titania always slept there for part of the night, wrapped in the shining, patterned skin of a snake. Oberon bent over her and put the juice on her eyes, saying:

“Whatever you see when you wake up,
Take it for your own true love.”

Now, it so happened that the first thing Titania saw when she woke was a stupid clown. He belonged to a group of players who had come into the wood to rehearse their play. Puck had run into this clown and had stuck an ass’s head on his shoulders, so that it looked as if it had always grown there. The moment Titania woke and saw this dreadful monster, she said, “What angel is this? Are you as wise as you are beautiful?”
“If I’m wise enough to find my way out of this wood, that’s all I need,” said the foolish clown.

“Don’t wish to leave this wood,” said Titania. The love-juice had her under its spell, and to her the clown seemed the loveliest, most delightful creature in the world. “I love you,” she went on. “Come along with me, and fairies will wait on you.”
Then she called four fairies, named Peaseblossom, Cobweb, Moth, and Mustardseed.

“You are to wait on this gentleman,” said the Queen. “Feed him apricots and dewberries, purple grapes, green figs, and mulberries. Steal honey-bags from the bumblebees for him, and fan the moonbeams away from his sleeping eyes with the wings of painted butterflies.”
“I will,” said one of the fairies, and all the others echoed, “I will.”
“Now sit beside me,” the Queen told the clown, “and let me stroke your dear cheeks, and tuck musk-roses into your smooth, sleek head, and kiss your handsome big ears, my gentle joy.”
“Where’s Peaseblossom?” called the clown with the ass’s head. He cared little for the Queen’s love, but he was very proud of having fairies at his service. “Ready,” said Peaseblossom.
“Scratch my head, Peaseblossom,” said the clown. “And where’s Cobweb?” “Ready,” said Cobweb.
“Kill me,” said the clown, “that red bumblebee on top of the thistle over there, and bring me his honey-bag. Where’s Mustardseed?”
“Ready,” said Mustardseed.
“Oh, I don’t want anything,” said the clown. “Just help Cobweb scratch. I must go to the barber’s, because I think my face is amazingly hairy.”
“Would you like something to eat?” asked the fairy Queen.
“I’d like some good dry oats,” said the clown—for his donkey’s head had given him a taste for donkey’s food—“and some hay after that.”
“Shall some of my fairies go and bring you fresh nuts from the squirrel’s house?” the Queen asked.
“I’d sooner have a good handful or two of dried peas,” said the clown. “But please see that none of your people bother me. I’m off to sleep.”
Then the Queen said, “And I will wrap you in my arms.”
So when Oberon came by, he found his beautiful Queen showering kisses and sweet words on a clown with a donkey’s head.

Before he freed her from the enchantment, he talked her into giving him the little Indian boy he wanted so much. Then he felt sorry for her and sprinkled the juice of the curing flower on her pretty eyes. In a moment she saw clearly the donkey-headed clown she had been loving, and she realized how foolish she had been.
Oberon lifted the ass’s head off the clown and left him to finish his nap, with his own silly head resting on the thyme and violets.
So everything was put right again. Oberon and Titania were fonder of each other than ever. Demetrius had eyes only for Helena, and Helena had never had eyes for anyone but Demetrius.
As for Hermia and Lysander, you could not have found a more loving couple in a day’s march, not even in a fairy wood.
So the four human lovers returned to Athens and were married. As for the fairy King and Queen, they live happily together in that same wood to this very day.

chapters.title: The Tempest
paragraphs: Prospero, the Duke of Milan, was a learned man who loved study and lived among his books. He left the running of his dukedom to his brother Antonio, whom he trusted completely. That trust was badly repaid. Antonio wanted to wear the duke’s crown himself, and to get it he would have killed his brother, if the people had not loved Prospero so much. Instead, with the help of Prospero’s great enemy Alonso, King of Naples, he got the dukedom into his own hands, with all its honor, power, and wealth. The two of them took Prospero out to sea, and when they were far from land they forced him into a little boat with no tackle, mast, or sail. In their cruelty and hatred they put his small daughter Miranda, not yet three years old, into the boat with him, and sailed away, leaving the two to their fate.

But one of the courtiers with Antonio stayed loyal to his rightful master. He could not save the duke from his enemies, but he could do a great deal to remind him that a subject’s love was still with him. This good lord, whose name was Gonzalo, secretly put some fresh water, food, and clothes into the boat, and also what Prospero valued most of all: some of his precious books.

The boat drifted to an island, and Prospero and his little girl came safely ashore. The island was enchanted. For years it had lain under the spell of a cruel witch named Sycorax, who had trapped all the good spirits she found there inside the trunks of trees. She had died shortly before Prospero was cast onto those shores, but the spirits, with Ariel as their chief, were still held in their prisons.

Prospero was a great magician, because during the years when he let his brother manage the affairs of Milan, he had given himself almost entirely to the study of magic. By his art he freed the imprisoned spirits and still kept them obedient to his will, and they were more truly his subjects than his people in Milan had ever been. He treated them kindly as long as they did what he asked, and he used his power over them wisely and well. Only one creature he found he had to treat harshly. This was Caliban, the son of the wicked old witch, a hideous, misshapen monster, horrible to look at, and vicious and brutal in all his habits.

When Miranda had grown into a sweet and lovely young woman, it happened that Antonio and Alonso were at sea together with Alonso’s brother Sebastian, his son Ferdinand, and old Gonzalo, and their ship came near Prospero’s island. Prospero knew they were there. By his art he raised a great storm, so fierce that even the sailors on board gave themselves up for lost. First of all, Prince Ferdinand leaped into the sea, and his father, in his grief, thought he had drowned. But Ariel brought him safely ashore. All the rest of the crew were washed overboard too, yet they were landed unhurt in different parts of the island. The good ship herself, which everyone believed was wrecked, lay at anchor in the harbor where Ariel had brought her. Such were the wonders Prospero and his spirits could perform.

While the tempest was still raging, Prospero showed his daughter the brave ship tossing in the hollow of the waves, and told her that it was full of living people like themselves. She felt pity for them and begged her father, who had raised the storm, to calm it. He told her not to be afraid, because he meant to save every one of them.

Then, for the first time, he told her the story of his life and of hers. He had raised this storm, he said, so that his enemies Antonio and Alonso, who were aboard that ship, would fall into his hands.

When he had finished his story, he charmed her to sleep, because Ariel was nearby and he had work for him to do. Ariel longed to be completely free and grumbled at being kept in drudgery. But Prospero sharply reminded him of all he had suffered while Sycorax ruled the island, and of the debt of gratitude he owed to the master who had put an end to that suffering. Ariel stopped complaining and promised faithfully to do whatever Prospero commanded.
“Do that,” said Prospero, “and in two days I will set you free.”
Then he told Ariel to take the shape of a water nymph and sent him to look for the young prince. Ariel, unseen by Ferdinand, hovered near him, singing as he went:

“Come to these yellow sands
And join your hands:
When you have curtsied and kissed
(The wild waves hush),
Dance lightly here and there;
And, sweet spirits, sing the refrain!”
Ferdinand followed the magic singing. The song changed to a solemn tune, and its words brought grief to his heart and tears to his eyes, for this is what they said:

“Your father lies five fathoms deep;
His bones have turned to coral.
Those pearls are what were his eyes,
Nothing of him will fade away,
But it undergoes a sea-change
Into something rich and strange.
Sea-nymphs ring his funeral bell each hour.
Listen! Now I hear them—ding dong bell!”

Singing like this, Ariel led the spellbound prince into the presence of Prospero and Miranda. And then, just as Prospero wanted, it all came to pass. Miranda had never, as far back as she could remember, seen any human being except her father. Now she looked at the young prince with reverence in her eyes and love in her secret heart.
“I could call him,” she said, “a divine thing, for I never saw anything in nature so noble!”
And Ferdinand, looking at her beauty with wonder and delight, cried out:
“Surely she is the goddess these airs wait on!”

He made no attempt to hide the passion she stirred in him. They had hardly spoken half a dozen sentences before he swore to make her his queen, if she was willing. Prospero was secretly delighted, but he pretended to be angry.

“You have come here as a spy,” he said to Ferdinand. “I will chain your neck and feet together, and you will live on freshwater mussels, withered roots, and husks, with sea-water to drink. Follow me.”

“No,” said Ferdinand, and drew his sword. But at that instant Prospero put a charm on him, so that he stood there like a statue, stiff as stone. Miranda, terrified, begged her father to have mercy on her lover. He harshly refused her, and made Ferdinand follow him to his cell. There he set the Prince to work, carrying thousands of heavy logs and stacking them in piles. Ferdinand obeyed patiently and felt that the sweet Miranda’s sympathy repaid his labor more than enough.

Out of pure pity she would have helped him with his hard work, but he would not let her. Yet he could not keep the secret of his love from her, and when she heard it she was overjoyed and promised to be his wife.
Then Prospero ended his servitude, and with a glad heart he agreed to their marriage.
“Take her,” he said. “She is your own.”

Meanwhile, in another part of the island, Antonio and Sebastian were plotting to murder Alonso, the King of Naples. They thought Ferdinand was dead, so Sebastian would become king when Alonso died. They would have carried out their wicked plan while their victim slept, but Ariel woke him in good time.

Ariel played many tricks on them. Once he set a banquet before them, and just as they were about to dig in, he appeared amid thunder and lightning in the shape of a harpy, and the banquet vanished at once. Then Ariel scolded them for their sins and vanished too.
By his enchantments Prospero drew them all into the grove outside his cell. There they waited, trembling and afraid, and by now they were bitterly sorry for their sins.
Prospero decided to use his magic power one last time. “And then,” he said, “I’ll break my staff, and deeper than any plummet ever sounded I’ll drown my book.”

So he made heavenly music sound in the air and appeared before them in his own shape, as the Duke of Milan. Because they were sorry, he forgave them, and he told them the story of his life since the day they had cruelly abandoned him and his baby daughter to the mercy of wind and waves. Alonso, who seemed the saddest of them all about his past crimes, was mourning the loss of his heir. But Prospero drew back a curtain and showed them Ferdinand and Miranda playing chess. Alonso was overjoyed to see his beloved son again. When he heard that the lovely girl Ferdinand was playing with was Prospero’s daughter, and that the young people had pledged themselves to each other, he said:
“Give me your hands. Let grief and sorrow ever fill the heart of anyone who does not wish you joy.”

So it all ended happily. The ship lay safe in the harbor, and the next day everyone set sail for Naples, where Ferdinand and Miranda were to be married. Ariel sent them calm seas and fair winds, and the wedding was a time of great rejoicing.

Then, after many years away, Prospero returned to his own dukedom, where his faithful subjects welcomed him with great joy. He practiced magic no more. His life was happy, not only because he had got back what was his, but chiefly because, when his bitterest enemies, who had done him deadly wrong, lay at his mercy, he took no revenge on them and nobly forgave them.
As for Ariel, Prospero set him free as air, so that he could wander wherever he liked and sing his sweet song with a light heart:

“Where the bee sucks, there I suck:
I lie inside a cowslip’s bell;
I rest there when the owls cry out.
I fly on the bat’s back
After summer ends, with joy:
With joy, with joy, I’ll live from now on,
Beneath the blossom on the bough.”

chapters.title: As You Like It
paragraphs: Once there was a wicked Duke named Frederick, who seized the dukedom that belonged to his brother and sent him into exile. His brother went to the Forest of Arden, where he lived as a bold forester, just as Robin Hood did in Sherwood Forest in merry England.

The banished Duke’s daughter Rosalind stayed behind with Celia, Frederick’s daughter, and the two loved each other more than most sisters do. One day there was a wrestling match at Court, and Rosalind and Celia went to watch. A famous wrestler named Charles was there, who had killed many men in contests of this kind. The young man he was to wrestle, Orlando, was so slender and so youthful that Rosalind and Celia felt sure he would be killed, as others had been. So they spoke to him and asked him not to attempt such a dangerous venture. But their words had only one effect: they made him want even more to do well in the fight, so that he could win praise from such sweet ladies.

Orlando’s own brother was keeping him out of his inheritance, just as Rosalind’s father had been robbed of his, and Orlando was so hurt by his brother’s unkindness that until he saw Rosalind he hardly cared whether he lived or died. Now the sight of the lovely Rosalind gave him new strength and courage. He fought so wonderfully that at last he threw Charles with a crash, and the wrestler had to be carried off the field. Duke Frederick admired his bravery and asked him his name.
“I am Orlando,” the young man replied, “the youngest son of Sir Rowland de Boys.”

While he lived, Sir Rowland de Boys had been a good friend to the banished Duke. So when Frederick learned whose son Orlando was, he was sorry, and refused to show him any favor. Rosalind, though, was delighted to hear that this handsome stranger was the son of her father’s old friend. As they were leaving, she looked back more than once to give the brave young man another kind word.
“Sir,” she said, taking a chain from her neck and handing it to him, “wear this for my sake. I would give you more, but my hand has nothing more to give.”
When Rosalind and Celia were alone, they began to talk about the handsome wrestler, and Rosalind admitted that she had fallen in love with him at first sight.
“Come, come,” said Celia, “wrestle with your feelings.”
“Oh,” Rosalind answered, “they have taken the side of a better wrestler than I am. Look, here comes the Duke.”
“His eyes are full of anger,” said Celia.
“Leave my Court at once,” he told Rosalind. “Why?” she asked.
“Never mind why,” the Duke answered. “You are banished. If you are found within twenty miles of my Court after ten days, you will die.”

So Rosalind set out to find her father, the banished Duke, in the Forest of Arden. Celia loved her too much to let her go alone. The journey was a rather dangerous one, so Rosalind, who was the taller of the two, disguised herself as a young countryman, and her cousin as a country girl. Rosalind decided they would go by the names Ganymede and Aliena. When they finally reached the Forest of Arden they were very tired. They were sitting on the grass when a countryman happened to pass, and Ganymede asked whether he could find them something to eat. He did, and he also told them that a shepherd’s flocks and house were for sale. They bought both and settled down in the forest as a shepherd and shepherdess.

Meanwhile Oliver had tried to kill his brother Orlando, and Orlando too had wandered into the forest. There he met the rightful Duke, who welcomed him kindly, and he stayed with him. Orlando could think of nothing but Rosalind. He went about the forest carving her name on trees, and he wrote love sonnets and hung them on the bushes, where Rosalind and Celia found them. One day Orlando met the two of them. He did not recognize Rosalind in her boy’s clothes, though he liked the pretty young shepherd, because he imagined he saw in him a likeness to the girl he loved.
“A foolish lover haunts these woods,” said Rosalind, “and he pins his sonnets to the trees. If I could find him, I would soon cure him of his folly.”

Orlando admitted that he was the foolish lover, and Rosalind said—“If you will come and see me every day, I will pretend to be Rosalind. I will play her part and be moody and contrary, as women often are, until I make you ashamed of loving her so foolishly.”

So every day he went to her house and happily said to her all the sweet things he would have said to Rosalind. And she had the fine, secret joy of knowing that every one of his loving words reached the right ears. In this way many days went by pleasantly.

One morning, as Orlando was on his way to visit Ganymede, he saw a man lying asleep on the ground. A lioness was crouching nearby, waiting for the sleeper to wake, since they say lions will not attack anything that is dead or sleeping. Then Orlando looked at the man and saw that it was his wicked brother Oliver, the one who had tried to kill him. He fought the lioness, killed her, and saved his brother’s life.

While Orlando was fighting the lioness, Oliver woke up. He saw the brother he had treated so cruelly saving him from a wild beast at the risk of his own life. This made him sorry for his wickedness, and he begged Orlando’s forgiveness. From then on the two were loving brothers. The lioness had hurt Orlando’s arm so badly that he could not go on to see the shepherd, so he sent his brother to ask Ganymede to come to him.

Oliver went and told the whole story to Ganymede and Aliena. Aliena was so touched by the manly way he owned up to his faults that she fell in love with him at once. But when Ganymede heard what danger Orlando had been in, she fainted. When she came to, she said, truthfully enough, “I should have been a woman, by rights.”
Oliver returned to his brother and repeated all this. “I love Aliena so dearly,” he said, “that I will hand my estates over to you, marry her, and stay here as a shepherd.”
“Have your wedding tomorrow,” said Orlando, “and I will invite the Duke and his friends.”
When Orlando told Ganymede that his brother was to be married the next day, he added, “Oh, how bitter it is to look at happiness through another man’s eyes.”
Then Rosalind, still in Ganymede’s clothes and speaking in his voice, answered—“If you really love Rosalind from the bottom of your heart, then when your brother marries Aliena, you shall marry her.”
The following day the Duke and his followers, along with Orlando, Oliver, and Aliena, gathered for the wedding.

Then Ganymede came in and asked the Duke, “If I bring your daughter Rosalind before you, will you let Orlando have her?” “Gladly,” said the Duke, “even if I had every kingdom on earth to give with her.”
“And you say you will take her when I bring her?” she asked Orlando. “I would,” he answered, “even if I were king of all kingdoms.”
Rosalind and Celia then left the room. Rosalind changed back into her pretty woman’s dress, and before long the two returned.
She turned to her father—“I give myself to you, for I am yours.” “If my eyes do not deceive me,” he said, “you are my daughter.”
Then she turned to Orlando—“I give myself to you, for I am yours.” “If my eyes do not deceive me,” he said, “you are my Rosalind.”
“If you are not he, I will have no father,” she told the Duke, and then she told Orlando, “If you are not he, I will have no husband.”

So Orlando and Rosalind were married, and Oliver and Celia too, and they all lived happily ever after, going back with the Duke to his kingdom. A holy hermit had shown Frederick how wicked he had been, and so he gave the dukedom back to his brother and went into a monastery himself to pray for forgiveness.

It was a merry wedding, held in the mossy clearings of the forest. A shepherd and shepherdess who had been friends with Rosalind during her time as a disguised shepherd were married the same day. The feasting and merrymaking were so lovely that they could have been found nowhere indoors, only out in the beautiful green wood.

chapters.title: The Winter’s Tale
paragraphs: Leontes was the King of Sicily, and his dearest friend was Polixenes, King of Bohemia. The two had grown up together and parted only when they became men and each had to go home and rule his own kingdom. Many years later, when both were married and each had a son, Polixenes came to stay with Leontes in Sicily.

Leontes had a violent temper and was rather foolish. He took it into his silly head that his wife Hermione liked Polixenes better than she liked him, her own husband. Once he had this idea, nothing could shake it loose. He ordered one of his lords, Camillo, to put poison in Polixenes’ wine. Camillo tried to talk him out of this wicked deed, but when he saw that the King would not be moved, he pretended to agree. Then he told Polixenes what was planned against him, and that same night they fled from the Court of Sicily and went back to Bohemia, where Camillo stayed on as Polixenes’ friend and adviser.
Leontes threw the Queen into prison, and her son, the heir to the throne, died of grief at seeing his mother treated so unjustly and so cruelly.

While the Queen was in prison she gave birth to a little baby. A friend of hers named Paulina dressed the baby in its finest clothes and carried it to the King. She thought the sight of his helpless little daughter would soften his heart toward his dear Queen, who had never done him any wrong and loved him far more than he deserved. But the King would not even look at the baby. He ordered Paulina’s husband to take it away on a ship and leave it in the most desolate and dreadful place he could find. Very much against his will, Paulina’s husband had to obey.

Then the poor Queen was brought out to be tried for treason, for loving Polixenes more than her King, when really she had never thought of anyone but her husband Leontes. Leontes had sent messengers to ask the god Apollo whether his cruel suspicions of the Queen were right. But he was too impatient to wait for them to return, and so they arrived in the middle of the trial. The Oracle said—
“Hermione is innocent, Polixenes is blameless, Camillo is a loyal subject, and Leontes is a jealous tyrant. The King shall live without an heir unless what is lost is found.”

Then a man came in and told them that the little Prince was dead. The poor Queen collapsed in a faint when she heard it, and the King finally saw how wicked and wrong he had been. He ordered Paulina and the ladies attending the Queen to carry her away and try to revive her. But in a few moments Paulina came back and told the King that Hermione was dead.

At last Leontes’ eyes were opened to his own foolishness. His Queen was dead, and the little daughter who might have been a comfort to him he had sent away to be eaten by wolves and kites. Life had nothing left to offer him. He gave himself up to grief and spent many sad years in prayer and remorse.

The baby Princess had been left on the seacoast of Bohemia, the very kingdom where Polixenes was king. Paulina’s husband never went home to tell Leontes where he had left the baby, because on his way back to the ship he met a bear and was torn to pieces. So that was the end of him.

But a shepherd found the poor abandoned baby. She was richly dressed and had some jewels with her, and a paper was pinned to her cloak saying that her name was Perdita and that her parents were noble.

The shepherd was a kind-hearted man. He took the little baby home to his wife, and the two of them raised her as their own child. She had no more schooling than a shepherd’s child usually gets, but she had inherited many graces and charms from her royal mother, and so she was quite unlike the other girls in the village where she lived.

One day Prince Florizel, the son of the good King of Bohemia, was hunting near the shepherd’s house and saw Perdita, who had by now grown into a charming young woman. He made friends with the shepherd without telling him he was the Prince. He said instead that his name was Doricles and that he was a private gentleman. Then, being deeply in love with the pretty Perdita, he came to see her almost every day.

The King could not understand what took his son away from home nearly every day, so he had people watch him. Then he found out that the heir of the King of Bohemia was in love with Perdita, the pretty shepherd girl. Polixenes wanted to see whether this was true, so he put on a disguise and went to the old shepherd’s house with the faithful Camillo, who was disguised too. They arrived during the sheep-shearing feast, and although they were strangers, they were given a warm welcome. There was dancing, and a peddler was selling ribbons, laces, and gloves, which the young men bought for their sweethearts.

Florizel and Perdita, however, took no part in all this merriment. They sat quietly together, talking. The King noticed Perdita’s charming manners and great beauty, never guessing that she was the daughter of his old friend Leontes. He said to Camillo—
“This is the prettiest low-born girl that ever ran on the green grass. Everything she does or seems has a touch of something greater than herself—too noble for a place like this.”
Camillo replied, “She really is the Queen of curds and cream.”

But then Florizel, who did not recognize his father, called on the strangers to witness his betrothal to the pretty shepherdess. The King made himself known and forbade the marriage. He added that if she ever saw Florizel again, he would kill her and her old father, the shepherd, and with that he left them. Camillo stayed behind, though, because he was charmed by Perdita and wanted to help her.

Camillo had known for a long time how sorry Leontes was for his foolish madness, and he longed to go back to Sicily and see his old master. Now he suggested that the young people go there and ask Leontes for his protection. So they went, and the shepherd went with them, bringing Perdita’s jewels, her baby clothes, and the paper he had found pinned to her cloak.
Leontes greeted them with great kindness. He was courteous to Prince Florizel, but he could not take his eyes off Perdita. He saw how closely she resembled Queen Hermione, and he kept saying—
“My daughter might have been such a sweet creature, if I had not cruelly sent her away from me.”

The old shepherd learned that the King had lost a baby daughter, left on the Bohemian coast, and he was certain that Perdita, whom he had raised, must be her. He told his story and showed the jewels and the paper, and the King realized that Perdita was truly his long-lost child. Joyfully he welcomed her, and he rewarded the good shepherd.
Polixenes had hurried after his son to put a stop to the match with Perdita. But once he learned that she was the daughter of his old friend, he gladly gave his consent.

Still, Leontes could not be happy. He remembered that his lovely Queen, who should have been at his side sharing his joy in his daughter’s happiness, was dead because of his unkindness. For a long time he could say nothing but—
“Oh, your mother! Your mother!” Then he would ask the King of Bohemia’s forgiveness, then kiss his daughter again, then the Prince Florizel, and then thank the old shepherd for all his goodness.

Then Paulina, who had stood high in the King’s favor all those years because of her kindness to the dead Queen Hermione, said—“I have a statue made in the likeness of the dead Queen. It took many years to make, and it is the work of the rare Italian master Giulio Romano. I keep it in a private house apart, and ever since you lost your Queen I have gone there two or three times a day. Would it please your Majesty to come and see the statue?”
So Leontes and Polixenes, Florizel and Perdita, Camillo, and their attendants went to Paulina’s house. There a heavy purple curtain hid an alcove, and Paulina put her hand on the curtain and said—

“She had no equal when she was alive, and I truly believe this likeness of her, now that she is dead, is finer than anything you have seen before, or anything a human hand has ever made. That is why I keep it here alone, apart from the rest. But here it is. Look, and tell me it is well done.”
With that she pulled back the curtain and showed them the statue. The King stared and stared at the beautiful figure of his dead wife, but he said nothing at all.
“I like your silence,” said Paulina. “It shows your wonder all the better. But speak. Isn’t it like her?”
“It is almost her very self,” said the King. “And yet, Paulina, Hermione did not have so many wrinkles. She was nowhere near as old as this looks.”
“Oh, not by much,” said Polixenes.
“Ah,” said Paulina, “that is the carver’s cleverness. He shows her to us as she would have looked if she had lived until now.”
Leontes kept his eyes on the statue and could not look away.
“If I had known,” said Paulina, “that this poor image would stir up so much grief and love in you, I would never have shown it to you.”
But he only answered, “Don’t draw the curtain.”
“No, don’t keep looking,” said Paulina, “or you will start to believe it moves.”
“Leave it! Leave it!” said the King. “Doesn’t it look as if it breathes?”
“I will close the curtain,” said Paulina. “In a moment you will believe it is alive.”
“Oh, dear Paulina,” said Leontes, “make me believe it for twenty years together.”
“If you can stand it,” said Paulina, “I will make the statue move. It will walk down and take you by the hand. Only you would think it was done by wicked magic.”
“Anything you can make her do, I will gladly watch,” said the King.

Then, while everyone there looked on in wonder, the statue stepped from its pedestal and came down the steps. It put its arms around the King’s neck, and he held her face and kissed her again and again, for this was no statue but the real, living Queen Hermione. Through Paulina’s kindness she had been living in hiding all those years. She had not revealed herself to her husband, though she knew he was sorry for what he had done, because she could not fully forgive him until she learned what had happened to her little baby.
Now that Perdita had been found, Hermione forgave her husband everything. Being together again felt to them like a new and beautiful marriage.
Florizel and Perdita were married, and they lived a long and happy life.
For Leontes, all his many years of suffering were repaid in that one moment, when after so much grief and pain he felt the arms of his true love around him again.

chapters.title: King Lear
paragraphs: King Lear was old and tired. He was weary of the work of ruling his kingdom and wanted only to spend his last days in peace, close to his three daughters. Two of them were married, to the Duke of Albany and the Duke of Cornwall. The Duke of Burgundy and the King of France were both asking for the hand of Cordelia, his youngest daughter.
Lear called his three daughters together and told them he planned to divide his kingdom among them. “But first,” he said, “I would like to know how much you love me.”

Goneril, who was in truth a very wicked woman and did not love her father at all, said she loved him more than words could say. She loved him more than her eyesight, more than space or freedom, more than life, grace, health, beauty and honor.
“I love you just as much as my sister does, and more,” declared Regan, “because nothing matters to me except my father’s love.”

Lear was delighted with what Regan said and turned to his youngest daughter, Cordelia. “Now, our joy, last but not least,” he said, “I have saved the best part of my kingdom for you. What do you have to say?”
“Nothing, my lord,” Cordelia answered.
“Nothing will come of nothing. Speak again,” said the King.
And Cordelia answered, “I love your Majesty as my duty requires—no more and no less.”
She said this because she was disgusted by the way her sisters spoke of their love, when they did not even have a proper sense of duty toward their old father.
“I am your daughter,” she went on. “You raised me and loved me, and I give you back the duties that are right and fitting: I obey you, love you, and honor you above all.”
Lear loved Cordelia best, and he had wanted her to make even grander declarations of love than her sisters. “Go,” he said. “From now on, be a stranger to my heart and to me.”

The Earl of Kent, one of Lear’s favorite courtiers and captains, tried to speak up for Cordelia, but Lear would not listen. He divided the kingdom between Goneril and Regan. He told them he would keep only a hundred knights for himself and would live with each daughter in turn.

When the Duke of Burgundy learned that Cordelia would receive no share of the kingdom, he gave up courting her. But the King of France was wiser, and he said, “Your daughter without a dowry, King, is Queen to us—to me, and to our fair France.”
“Take her, take her,” said the King, “for I never want to see her face again.”

So Cordelia became Queen of France, and the Earl of Kent, for daring to take her side, was banished from the kingdom. The King now went to stay with his daughter Goneril. She had already taken everything her father had to give, and now she begrudged him even the hundred knights he had kept. She was harsh and disrespectful to him, and her servants either refused to follow his orders or pretended not to hear them.

Now the Earl of Kent, when he was banished, had pretended to leave for another country. Instead he came back disguised as a servant and went into the King’s service. So the King now had two friends: the Earl of Kent, whom he knew only as his servant, and his Fool, who stayed loyal to him. Goneril told her father bluntly that his knights did nothing but fill her Court with noise and feasting, and she asked him to keep just a few old men around him, men as old as himself.
“My followers are men who know every part of their duty,” said Lear. “Goneril, I will trouble you no more—but I still have another daughter.”

His horses were saddled, and he set out with his followers for Regan’s castle. But Regan, who had once outdone her sister in declaring her devotion to the King, now seemed to outdo her in disrespect. She said fifty knights were too many to attend him. Goneril, who had rushed there to stop Regan from showing the old King any kindness, said five were too many, since her own servants could attend him.

When Lear saw that all they truly wanted was to be rid of him, he walked out on them. The night was wild and stormy. He wandered over the heath half mad with misery, and the only one with him was the poor Fool. Before long his servant, the good Earl of Kent, found him and finally talked him into lying down in a miserable little hovel. At daybreak the Earl of Kent took his royal master to Dover, then hurried to the Court of France to tell Cordelia everything that had happened.

Cordelia’s husband gave her an army, and she landed at Dover with it. There she found poor King Lear, wandering through the fields in a crown of nettles and weeds. They brought him back, fed him and gave him clothes, and Cordelia came to him and kissed him.
“You must be patient with me,” said Lear. “Forget and forgive. I am old and foolish.”
And now at last he knew which of his children had loved him best, and which one deserved his love.

Goneril and Regan joined their armies to fight Cordelia’s army, and they won, and Cordelia and her father were thrown into prison. Then Goneril’s husband, the Duke of Albany, a good man who had never known how wicked his wife was, heard the whole truth. When Goneril saw that her husband knew her for the wicked woman she was, she killed herself. A little earlier, out of jealousy, she had given her sister Regan a deadly poison.

But the sisters had arranged for Cordelia to be hanged in prison, and although the Duke of Albany sent messengers at once, they came too late. The old King came staggering into the Duke of Albany’s tent, carrying the body of his dear daughter Cordelia in his arms.
Soon afterward, with loving words for her still on his lips, he collapsed with her in his arms and died.

chapters.title: Twelfth Night
paragraphs: Orsino, the Duke of Illyria, was deeply in love with a beautiful Countess named Olivia. But all his love was wasted, because she scorned his courtship. When her brother died, she sent the Duke’s messenger back with a message for his master: for seven years she would not let even the air see her face, but would go veiled like a nun. She did all this out of love for her dead brother, which she meant to keep fresh and lasting in her sad memory.

The Duke longed for someone he could tell his sorrow to, and with whom he could go over the story of his love again and again. And chance gave him such a companion. About this time a fine ship was wrecked on the coast of Illyria. Among those who reached land safely were the captain and a young girl named Viola. She was not at all thankful to have been saved from the dangers of the sea, because she feared that her twin brother Sebastian had drowned. He was as dear to her as the heart in her chest, and so like her that, apart from the difference in their clothes, you could hardly tell one from the other. To comfort her, the captain told her he had seen her brother tie himself “to a strong mast that lived upon the sea,” so there was hope that he might be saved.

Viola then asked whose country she was in. She learned that the young Duke Orsino ruled there and was as noble in character as in name. She decided to disguise herself in men’s clothes and ask him for a job as a page.

She succeeded in this, and from then on, day after day, she had to listen to the story of Orsino’s love. At first she felt true sympathy for him, but soon her sympathy turned into love. At last it occurred to Orsino that his hopeless courtship might go better if he sent this pretty boy to woo Olivia for him. Viola went on this errand unwillingly. When she reached the house, Malvolio, Olivia’s steward, a vain, bossy man who was, as his mistress told him, sick with self-love, refused the messenger entry.

But Viola, who was now called Cesario, would not accept a refusal and swore she would speak with the Countess. Olivia heard how her orders had been defied, and she was curious to see this daring youth. She said, “We’ll hear Orsino’s message once more.”

When Viola was let in to see her and the servants had been sent away, she listened patiently to the reproaches this bold messenger from the Duke heaped upon her. And as she listened, she fell in love with the supposed Cesario. After Cesario left, Olivia longed to send some token of love after him. So she called Malvolio and told him to follow the boy.
“He left this ring behind,” she said, taking one from her finger. “Tell him I want nothing to do with it.”

Malvolio did as he was told. Viola knew perfectly well that she had left no ring behind, and with a woman’s quick sense she saw that Olivia loved her. Then she went back to the Duke, very sad at heart for the man she loved, for Olivia, and for herself.
She could offer Orsino only cold comfort. He now tried to ease the pain of scorned love by listening to sweet music, with Cesario standing at his side.
“Ah,” the Duke said to his page that night, “you have been in love too.”
“A little,” Viola answered.
“What kind of woman is she?” he asked.
“She has your coloring,” she answered.
“How old, in faith?” was his next question.
To this came the charming reply, “Close to your age, my lord.”
“Too old, by Heaven!” cried the Duke. “A woman should always choose someone older than herself.”
And Viola said very meekly, “I think so too, my lord.”
Soon afterward Orsino begged Cesario to visit Olivia once more and plead his cause. But Viola, hoping to talk him out of it, said—
“What if some lady loved you the way you love Olivia?”
“Ah! That cannot be,” said the Duke.
“But I know,” Viola went on, “what love a woman may have for a man. My father had a daughter who loved a man, just as, perhaps,” she added, blushing, “I would love your lordship if I were a woman.”
“And what is her story?” he asked.

“A blank, my lord,” Viola answered. “She never told her love. She let it stay hidden, like a worm in a bud, feeding on her rosy cheek. She pined away in thought, and with a green and yellow melancholy she sat, like Patience on a monument, smiling at grief. Wasn’t that love indeed?”
“But did your sister die of her love, my boy?” the Duke asked. And Viola, who all this time had been telling him of her own love for him in this charming way, said—
“I am the only daughter my father has, and the only son too—Sir, shall I go to the lady?”
“Go to her quickly,” said the Duke, instantly forgetting the whole story, “and give her this jewel.”
So Viola went, and this time poor Olivia could not hide her love. She confessed it openly with such passionate honesty that Viola left her in haste, saying—
“Never again will I lament my master’s tears to you.”

But in making this vow, Viola did not know how tenderly she would feel for the suffering of others. So when Olivia, in the violence of her love, sent a messenger begging Cesario to visit her once more, Cesario did not have the heart to refuse.

But the favors Olivia gave to this mere page made Sir Andrew Aguecheek jealous. He was a foolish, rejected suitor of hers, then staying at her house with her merry old uncle, Sir Toby. Sir Toby dearly loved a practical joke, and he knew Sir Andrew was an utter coward. He thought that if he could arrange a duel between Sir Andrew and Cesario, there would be rare sport indeed. So he talked Sir Andrew into sending a challenge, which he delivered to Cesario himself. The poor page, in great terror, said—
“I will go back to the house. I am no fighter.”
“You will not go back to that house,” said Sir Toby, “until you have fought me.”

Sir Toby looked like a very fierce old gentleman, so Viola decided it was best to wait for Sir Andrew. When he finally appeared, badly frightened, if the truth were known, she drew her sword with trembling hands, and Sir Andrew, just as afraid, copied her. Luckily for them both, at that moment some officers of the Court arrived and stopped the duel. Viola gladly slipped away as fast as she could, while Sir Toby called after her—
“A very worthless boy, and more of a coward than a hare!”

Meanwhile, Sebastian had escaped all the dangers of the sea and landed safely in Illyria, where he decided to make his way to the Duke’s Court. On the way he passed Olivia’s house just after Viola had left it in such a hurry, and who should he run into but Sir Andrew and Sir Toby. Sir Andrew mistook Sebastian for the cowardly Cesario. He gathered all his courage, walked up to him and struck him, saying, “That’s for you.”

“Take that, and that, and that!” said Sebastian, hitting back much harder, again and again, until Sir Toby rushed in to rescue his friend. But Sebastian wrenched himself out of Sir Toby’s grip and drew his sword, ready to fight them both. Just then Olivia herself, who had heard about the quarrel, came running in and scolded them bitterly, sending Sir Toby and his friend away. Then she turned to Sebastian, whom she also took for Cesario, and with many charming words begged him to come into the house with her.

Sebastian was half in a daze and completely delighted by her beauty and grace, and he agreed at once. Olivia was in such a hurry that the two were married that very day, before she found out he was not Cesario, and before Sebastian could be sure whether or not he was dreaming.

Meanwhile Orsino heard how badly Cesario was doing with Olivia, so he went to see her himself and took Cesario along. Olivia met them both outside her door. Seeing, as she thought, her husband standing there, she scolded him for leaving her. To the Duke she said that his courtship was as rich and wholesome to her as howling after music.
“Still so cruel?” said Orsino.
“Still so faithful,” she answered.
Orsino’s anger now turned into cruelty. He swore that to take revenge on her he would kill Cesario, whom he knew she loved. “Come, boy,” he said to the page.
Viola followed him as he walked away, saying, “To give you peace, I would gladly die a thousand deaths.”
Olivia was seized by a great fear, and she cried out, “Cesario, husband, stay!”
“Her husband?” the Duke asked angrily.
“No, my lord, not I,” said Viola.
“Bring the holy father here,” cried Olivia.
The priest who had married Sebastian and Olivia came in and declared that Cesario was the bridegroom.
“Oh, you deceiving cub!” the Duke exclaimed. “Goodbye, and keep her, but go where you and I will never meet again.”
Just then Sir Andrew came up with a bleeding head, complaining that Cesario had broken it, and Sir Toby’s head too.
“I never hurt you,” said Viola very firmly. “You drew your sword on me, but I spoke to you politely and did not harm you.”
Yet for all her protests, nobody there believed her. But then Sebastian walked in, and in an instant everyone’s mind was filled with wonder instead.
“I am sorry, madam,” he said to his wife, “that I have hurt your relative. Forgive me, sweet one, for the sake of the vows we made to each other so recently.”
“One face, one voice, one costume, and yet two people!” cried the Duke, glancing from Viola to Sebastian and back again.
“An apple split in two,” said someone who knew Sebastian, “is no more alike than these two. Which one is Sebastian?”

“I never had a brother,” said Sebastian. “I had a sister, whom the blind waves and surges swallowed up.” Then he said to Viola, “If you were a woman, I would let my tears fall on your cheek and say, ‘Three times welcome, drowned Viola!’”
Viola was overjoyed to see her dear brother alive, and she admitted that she was in fact his sister, Viola. As she spoke, Orsino felt the kind of pity that is close to love.
“Boy,” he said, “you told me a thousand times that you would never love a woman the way you love me.”
“And I will swear all those words again,” Viola answered, “and keep all those vows true.”
“Give me your hand,” Orsino cried happily. “You will be my wife, and the queen of my heart.”
So gentle Viola was made happy. Olivia found in Sebastian a faithful lover and a good husband, and he found in her a true and loving wife.

chapters.title: Much Ado About Nothing
paragraphs: There is a town in Sicily called Messina, and several hundred years ago it was the scene of a strange storm in a teacup.

It began with sunshine. Don Pedro, Prince of Arragon in Spain, had won such a complete victory over his enemies that even the land they came from has been forgotten. After the hardships of war he felt cheerful and playful, so he came to Messina for a holiday. With him in his company were his stepbrother Don John and two young Italian lords, Benedick and Claudio.

Benedick was a merry chatterbox who had made up his mind to stay a bachelor. Claudio, by contrast, had barely arrived in Messina before he fell in love with Hero, the daughter of Leonato, the Governor of Messina.
One July day a perfumer named Borachio was burning dried lavender in a stuffy room of Leonato’s house when the sound of voices drifted in through the open window.
“Tell me honestly what you think of Hero,” Claudio asked, and Borachio settled down to listen in comfort.
“Too short and too brown to be praised,” was Benedick’s answer, “but change her color or her height and you would spoil her.”
“To my eyes she is the sweetest of women,” said Claudio.

“Not to mine,” Benedick shot back, “and I don’t need spectacles to see. Set her beside her cousin, and she is like the last day of December next to the first of May. Unfortunately, Lady Beatrice is a fury.”

Beatrice, Leonato’s niece, loved to make clever, stinging remarks about Benedick, and he in turn called her Dear Lady Disdain. She used to claim that a dancing star had watched over her birth, so dullness was out of the question for her.
Claudio and Benedick had not finished their talk when Don Pedro strolled over and asked in a friendly way, “Well, gentlemen, what is the secret?”
“I am longing,” Benedick answered, “for your Grace to order me to tell.”
“Then I order you, on your duty as my subject, to tell me,” said Don Pedro, playing along with his mood.
“I can keep as quiet as a mute,” Benedick said to Claudio, as if sorry, “but his Grace commands me to speak.” Then he said to Don Pedro, “Claudio is in love with Hero, Leonato’s short daughter.”

Don Pedro was pleased, because he admired Hero and was fond of Claudio. After Benedick had gone, he said to Claudio, “Stay firm in your love for Hero, and I will help you win her. Tonight her father is giving a masquerade ball. I will pretend to be Claudio and tell her how much Claudio loves her. If she is pleased, I will go to her father and ask his permission for your marriage.”
Most men would rather court a lady themselves. But when the lady is the only daughter of a Governor, you can count yourself lucky if a prince is willing to make your case for you.

So Claudio was lucky, but he was unlucky too, because he had an enemy who seemed to be a friend. This enemy was Don Pedro’s stepbrother Don John, who was jealous of Claudio because Don Pedro liked Claudio better than him.
Borachio took the interesting talk he had overheard straight to Don John, and told him all of it.
When Borachio had said his piece, Don John remarked, “I mean to enjoy that masquerade myself.”
When the night of the masquerade came, Don Pedro put on a mask and played the part of Claudio. He asked Hero whether she would take a walk with him.
The pair strolled off together. Don John then approached Claudio and said, “You are Signor Benedick, I think?” “I am,” Claudio fibbed.
“In that case I would be grateful,” said Don John, “if you would use whatever influence you have with my brother to talk him out of loving Hero. She is beneath him in rank.”
“How do you know he loves her?” asked Claudio.
“I heard him swear that he does,” was the answer, and Borachio chimed in, “So did I.”
That left Claudio alone with his thoughts, and he thought that his Prince had betrayed him. “Farewell, Hero,” he muttered. “I was a fool to trust a go-between.”
Elsewhere in the room, Beatrice and Benedick, who was wearing a mask, were busy trading sharp opinions.
“Did Benedick ever make you laugh?” she asked.
“Who is Benedick?” he asked.
“A Prince’s jester,” replied Beatrice, and she said it so sharply that afterward he declared, “I would not marry her even if her estate were the Garden of Eden.”

Yet neither Beatrice nor Benedick did the most important talking at the masquerade. That was done by Don Pedro, who followed his plan to the letter. He made the light return to Claudio’s face in a moment, simply by coming up to him with Leonato and Hero and asking, “Claudio, how soon would you like to go to church?”
“Tomorrow,” was the quick answer. “Time limps on crutches until I marry Hero.”
“Allow her a week, my dear son,” said Leonato. Claudio’s heart pounded with happiness.
“Now,” said the kindly Don Pedro, “we need to find a wife for Signor Benedick. That is a job for Hercules.”
“Count me in,” said Leonato, “even if it costs me ten nights without sleep.”
Hero then said, “My lord, I will do my best to find Beatrice a good husband.”
So, amid happy laughter, the masquerade ended, having taught Claudio a lesson for nothing.

Borachio cheered up Don John by laying out a plan. He was sure it would convince both Claudio and Don Pedro that Hero was a fickle girl who kept two strings to her bow. Don John agreed to this plan of hate.

Don Pedro, meanwhile, had thought up a clever plan of love. “Suppose,” he said to Leonato, “that we pretend, when Beatrice is close enough to overhear, that Benedick is pining for her love. She will pity him, notice his good qualities, and love him. And suppose that, when Benedick thinks we don’t know he is listening, we say how sad it is that the beautiful Beatrice should love a heartless scoffer like Benedick. Then he will surely be on his knees before her within a week or less.”
Not long after, Benedick sat reading in a summerhouse. Claudio and Leonato took seats just outside it, and Claudio began, “Your daughter mentioned a letter that she wrote.”

“Oh, the letter!” cried Leonato. “She will rise twenty times a night to scribble goodness knows what. Hero once peeked and saw ‘Benedick and Beatrice’ written on the page, and then Beatrice tore the whole sheet to pieces.”
“Hero told me,” said Claudio, “that she cried out, ‘Oh, sweet Benedick!’”

Benedick was deeply moved by this far-fetched tale, and being vain, he believed every word. “She is fair and good,” he told himself. “I mustn’t look proud. I can feel that I love her. Of course people will laugh, but their paper bullets can’t hurt me.”
Right then Beatrice arrived at the summerhouse. “I have come against my will,” she said, “to tell you that dinner is ready.”
“Fair Beatrice, I thank you,” said Benedick.
“It cost me no more effort to come than it costs you to thank me,” she replied, hoping to chill him.
It did not chill him; it warmed him instead. He wrung from her rude words the idea that she was thrilled to come to him.

Hero had taken on the job of melting Beatrice’s heart, and she did not bother to look for an occasion. One day she simply said to her maid Margaret, “Run into the parlor and whisper to Beatrice that Ursula and I are talking about her in the orchard.”
With that done, Hero felt every bit as sure that Beatrice would catch what was meant for her ears as if she had arranged to meet her cousin.
A bower stood in the orchard, sheltered from the sun by honeysuckle vines. A few minutes after Margaret left on her errand, Beatrice slipped inside.
“Are you really certain,” Ursula, one of Hero’s ladies, asked, “that Benedick loves Beatrice so devotedly?”
“So the Prince and my betrothed say,” Hero replied, “and they wanted me to tell her, but I said, ‘No! Let Benedick get over it.’”
“Why did you say that?”

“Because Beatrice is much too proud. Her eyes flash with scorn and contempt, and she thinks too highly of herself to love anyone. I wouldn’t want her to make fun of poor Benedick’s love. I would sooner watch him wither away like a fire that has been smothered.”
“I don’t agree with you,” said Ursula. “I think your cousin is too clear-sighted not to see Benedick’s worth.” “He is the one man in Italy, apart from Claudio,” said Hero.

The two then walked out of the orchard. Beatrice came out of the summerhouse, thrilled and tender, and told herself, “Poor dear Benedick, be true to me, and your love will tame this wild heart of mine.”
Now we go back to the plan of hate.
On the night before the day set for Claudio’s wedding, Don John walked into a room where Don Pedro and Claudio were talking and asked Claudio whether he really meant to be married tomorrow.
“You know he does!” said Don Pedro.
“He may feel differently,” said Don John, “after he sees what I am about to show him, if he will come with me.”
They followed him into the garden, and there they saw a lady leaning out of Hero’s window, speaking words of love to Borachio.
Claudio thought the lady was Hero and said, “I will shame her for this tomorrow!” Don Pedro thought it was Hero too, but it was not Hero. It was Margaret.
When Claudio and Don Pedro left the garden, Don John chuckled silently and gave Borachio a purse holding a thousand ducats.
The money put Borachio in a very merry mood, and as he walked down the street with his friend Conrade, he bragged about his wealth and the man who had given it to him, and told what he had done.

A watchman overheard them and decided that a man who had been paid a thousand ducats for villainy was worth arresting. So he took Borachio and Conrade into custody, and they spent the rest of the night in prison.

Before noon the next day, half the nobility of Messina was at church. Hero thought it was her wedding day, and there she stood in her wedding dress, with no cloud on her pretty face or in her honest, shining eyes.
The priest was Friar Francis.
The Friar turned to Claudio and asked, “My lord, have you come here to marry this lady?” “No!” Claudio answered flatly.
Leonato assumed he was quibbling about grammar. “Friar, what he ought to have said,” he put in, “is ‘I have come to be married to her.’”
Then Friar Francis asked Hero, “Lady, have you come here to be married to this Count?” “Yes,” Hero replied.
“If either of you knows of any obstacle to this marriage, I order you to say so,” said the Friar.
“Can you think of one, Hero?” Claudio asked. “Not one,” she said.
“And you, Count?” the Friar pressed. “I dare answer for him, ‘None,’” said Leonato.
Claudio exclaimed bitterly, “Oh! What will men not dare to say!” Then he continued, “Father, will you give me your daughter?” “As freely,” replied Leonato, “as God gave her to me.”
“And what can I give in return,” Claudio asked, “that is worthy of such a gift?” “Nothing,” said Don Pedro, “unless you hand the gift back to the one who gave it.”
“Sweet Prince, you teach me,” said Claudio. “Here, Leonato, take her back.”
More cruel words came pouring out of Claudio, Don Pedro and Don John after these.

The church no longer seemed holy. Hero defended herself as long as she could, and then she fainted. All her accusers left the church except her father, who had been fooled by the charges against her and cried out, “Away from her! Let her die!”
But Friar Francis, with eyes that could see into the soul, saw that Hero was blameless. “She is innocent,” he said. “A thousand signs have told me so.”

Under his kindly gaze Hero came back to herself. Her father was flustered and angry and could not tell what to believe. The Friar said, “Shame has left her like one who is dead. Let us give out that she is dead, until the truth comes out and slander turns into regret.”
“The Friar gives good advice,” said Benedick. Then Hero was led away to a place of retreat, and Beatrice and Benedick were left alone in the church.
Benedick knew she had been weeping bitterly for a long time. “I truly believe your fair cousin has been wronged,” he said. She kept on weeping.
“Isn’t it odd,” Benedick asked her gently, “that there is nothing in the world I love as much as you?”
“It would be just as easy for me to say there is nothing I love as much as you,” said Beatrice, “but I won’t say it. I am grieving for my cousin.”
“Tell me what I can do for her,” said Benedick. “Kill Claudio,” she said.
“Ha! Not for all the world,” said Benedick. “By refusing, you kill me,” said Beatrice. “Goodbye.”
“Enough! I will challenge him,” cried Benedick.
During this scene Borachio and Conrade were in prison. There a constable named Dogberry questioned them.
The watchman testified that Borachio had said he had been paid a thousand ducats to conspire against Hero.

Leonato was not at this hearing, but he was now fully convinced that Hero was innocent. He played the grieving father convincingly. When Don Pedro and Claudio came to see him in a friendly way, he told the Italian, “You have slandered my child to death, and I challenge you to a duel.”
“I can’t fight an old man,” said Claudio.
“You could kill a young girl,” Leonato sneered, and Claudio turned red.
One angry word led to another, and Don Pedro and Claudio were both stinging from them when Leonato stormed out of the room and Benedick walked in.
“That old man,” said Claudio, “very nearly snapped my nose off.”
“You are a villain!” Benedick said curtly. “Fight me, at any time and with any weapon you like, or I will call you a coward.”
Claudio was stunned, but he answered, “I’ll meet you. No one will ever say I can’t carve a calf’s head.”
Benedick smiled. It was time for Don Pedro to receive the officials, so the Prince took his seat on the chair of state and got ready to dispense justice.
Before long the door opened, and Dogberry came in with his prisoners.
“What crime,” asked Don Pedro, “are these men accused of?”
Borachio decided this was a good moment to confess everything. He put all the blame on Don John, who had vanished. “Now that the lady Hero is dead,” he said, “I want nothing but a murderer’s reward.”
Claudio listened in agony and deep remorse.
When Leonato came back into the room, he told him, “This wretch proves your daughter was innocent. Name your revenge.”
“Leonato,” said Don Pedro humbly, “I am ready to accept any penance you set.”

“Then I ask you both,” said Leonato, “to announce my daughter’s innocence, and to honor her tomb by singing her praises in front of it. And to you, Claudio, I say this: my brother has a daughter who looks so much like Hero that she could be her copy. Marry her, and my desire for revenge ends.”

“Noble sir,” said Claudio, “I am at your service.” Then Claudio went to his room and wrote a solemn song. He went to the church with Don Pedro and his attendants and sang it in front of the monument of Leonato’s family. When he finished, he said, “Good night, Hero. I will do this every year.”

After that, he made ready, gravely, as a gentleman should whose heart belonged to Hero, to marry a girl he did not love. He was told to meet her at Leonato’s house, and he arrived there faithfully, on time.
He was shown into a room, and Antonio (Leonato’s brother) came in after him with several masked ladies. Friar Francis, Leonato and Benedick were already there.
Antonio led one of the ladies over to Claudio.
“My dear,” said the young man, “let me see your face.”
“First swear to marry her,” said Leonato.
“Your hand, please,” Claudio said to the lady. “I swear before this holy friar that I will marry you, if you are willing to be my wife.”
“When I was alive, I was your wife,” said the lady, pulling off her mask.
“Another Hero!” Claudio cried.
“Hero died,” Leonato explained, “only as long as slander lived.”
The Friar was about to marry the reunited couple, but Benedick cut in. “Wait, Friar. Which of these ladies is Beatrice?”
At this, Beatrice took off her mask, and Benedick said, “You love me, don’t you?”
“Only so-so,” she replied. “Do you love me?”
“So-so,” Benedick answered.
“I was told you were nearly dying for me,” said Beatrice.
“I was told the very same about you,” said Benedick.

“Here is your own handwriting, proof that you love her,” said Claudio, and he held up a feeble sonnet that Benedick had written to his sweetheart. “And here,” said Hero, “is a poem in praise of Benedick, which I took out of Beatrice’s pocket.”
“A miracle!” cried Benedick. “Our own handwriting testifies against our hearts! Come, Beatrice, I will marry you.”
“You will be my husband, to save your life,” she shot back.
Benedick kissed her full on the lips, and the Friar married them, after first marrying Claudio and Hero.
“How is Benedick, the married man?” asked Don Pedro.

“Too happy to be made unhappy,” Benedick replied. “Joke all you like. As for you, Claudio, I had hoped to run you through with my sword, but now that you are my relative, live in good health and love my cousin.”
