“My club was in love with you, Benedick, until today,” said Claudio. But Benedick said, “Come, come, let’s dance.”
And dance they did. Even the news that Don John had been captured could not slow the flying feet of the happy lovers, for there is no sweetness in revenge on a wicked man who has failed in his harm.

chapters.title: Romeo and Juliet
paragraphs: Once upon a time, in Verona, there lived two great families, the Montagus and the Capulets. Both were rich, and I suppose they were as sensible about most things as other rich people. But about one thing they were truly foolish. The two families had an ancient quarrel, and instead of settling it like reasonable people, they made a kind of pet of it and refused to let it die. So if a Montagu met a Capulet in the street, he would not speak to him, and a Capulet would not speak to a Montagu either. Or if they did speak, it was to say rude and nasty things, and these often ended in a fight. Their relatives and servants were just as foolish, so street brawls, duels and other unpleasantness of that sort kept springing out of the quarrel between Montagu and Capulet.

Now Lord Capulet, the head of that family, gave a party, a grand supper and a dance. He was so generous a host that he said anyone at all could come, except (of course) the Montagues. But there was a young Montagu named Romeo who badly wanted to be there, because Rosaline, the lady he loved, had been invited. She had never been the least bit kind to him, and he had no good reason to love her. The truth was that he wanted to love somebody, and since he had not yet met the right lady, he had to love the wrong one. So he came to the Capulets’ grand party with his friends Mercutio and Benvolio.

Old Capulet welcomed him and his two friends warmly, and young Romeo wandered through the crowd of elegant guests. They were dressed in velvets and satins, the men with jeweled sword hilts and collars, the ladies with glittering gems on their breasts and arms and precious stones set in their bright belts. Romeo was in his finest clothes too. He wore a black mask over his eyes and nose, but everyone could tell from his mouth, his hair and the way he held his head that he was twelve times handsomer than anyone else in the room.

Soon he saw among the dancers a lady so beautiful and so lovable that from that moment he never gave another thought to the Rosaline he had believed he loved. He watched this other fair lady moving in the dance in her white satin and pearls, and the whole world seemed empty and worthless to him next to her. He was saying something like this aloud when Tybalt, Lady Capulet’s nephew, heard his voice and knew it was Romeo. Tybalt was furious. He went straight to his uncle and told him that a Montagu had come to the feast uninvited. But old Capulet was too fine a gentleman to be rude to anyone under his own roof, and he told Tybalt to be quiet. The young man only waited for a chance to pick a quarrel with Romeo.

Meanwhile Romeo made his way to the fair lady, told her in sweet words that he loved her, and kissed her. Just then her mother called her away, and Romeo learned that the lady he had set his heart on was Juliet, the daughter of Lord Capulet, his sworn enemy. He left, full of sorrow, but loving her no less.
Then Juliet said to her nurse:
“Who is that gentleman who wouldn’t dance?”
“That is Romeo, a Montagu, the only son of your great enemy,” the nurse replied.

Then Juliet went up to her room and looked out of her window over the lovely green-gray garden, where the moon was shining. Romeo was hiding in that garden among the trees, because he could not bear to leave without trying to see her once more. So she, not knowing he was there, spoke her secret thoughts out loud and told the quiet garden how much she loved Romeo.

Romeo heard her and was overjoyed. Hidden below, he looked up and saw her fair face in the moonlight, framed by the flowering vines that grew around her window. As he looked and listened, he felt as if he had been swept away in a dream and set down by some magician in that beautiful, enchanted garden.
“Ah, Romeo, why must you be Romeo?” said Juliet. “I love you, so why should a name matter?”

“Call me only love, and I will be baptized anew. From now on I will never be Romeo,” he cried, stepping out of the shade of the cypresses and oleanders that had hidden him, into the bright white moonlight.

At first she was frightened, but when she saw that it was Romeo himself and not a stranger, she was glad too. He stood in the garden below and she leaned from the window, and they talked together for a long time, each trying to find the sweetest words in the world, the kind of lovely talk that lovers have. Everything they said, and the sweet music their voices made together, is written down in a golden book, where you children may read it for yourselves some day.
Time passed as quickly as it does for people in love who are together, so that when it was time to part, it felt as if they had only just met. In fact, they hardly knew how to say good-bye.
“I will send word to you tomorrow,” said Juliet.
At last, still lingering and longing to stay, they said their farewells.
Juliet went in, and a dark curtain fell across her bright window. Romeo wandered off through the hushed, dew-wet garden like someone walking in a dream.
Very early the next morning, Romeo went to Friar Laurence, a priest. He told him the whole story and begged him to marry him to Juliet without delay. After some talk, the priest agreed to do it.

That day Juliet sent her old nurse to Romeo to ask what he meant to do. The old woman carried back word that all was well and everything was ready for the marriage of Juliet and Romeo the next morning.
The young lovers were afraid to ask their parents for permission to marry, as young people ought to, because of the foolish old feud between the Capulets and the Montagues.

Friar Laurence was willing to help the young lovers in secret, because he thought that once they were married their parents could soon be told, and that the marriage might bring the old quarrel to a happy end.

So early the following morning, Romeo and Juliet were married in Friar Laurence’s cell, and said good-bye with tears and kisses. Romeo promised to come to the garden that evening. The nurse made a rope ladder ready to lower from the window, so that Romeo could climb up and talk quietly with his dear wife, just the two of them.
But that very day something terrible happened.

Tybalt, who had been so angry that Romeo came to the Capulets’ feast, met Romeo in the street with his two friends, Mercutio and Benvolio. He called Romeo a villain and demanded that he fight. Romeo did not want to fight Juliet’s cousin, but Mercutio drew his sword, and he and Tybalt fought, and Mercutio was killed. When Romeo saw his friend lying dead, he forgot everything but his fury at the man who had killed him, and he fought Tybalt until Tybalt fell dead.

So on the very day of his wedding Romeo killed his dear Juliet’s cousin, and he was sentenced to be banished. Poor Juliet and her young husband did meet that night. He climbed the rope ladder among the flowers and found her window, but it was a sad meeting, and they parted with bitter tears and heavy hearts, because they could not know when they would meet again.

Now Juliet’s father, who of course had no idea that she was married, wanted her to wed a gentleman named Paris. When she refused, he grew so angry that she hurried off to ask Friar Laurence what to do. He advised her to pretend to agree, and then he said:

“I will give you a potion that will make you seem dead for two days. When they take you to the church, it will be to bury you and not to marry you. They will lay you in the vault, believing you are dead, and before you wake, Romeo and I will be there to look after you. Will you do this, or are you afraid?”

“I will do it. Don’t talk to me about being afraid!” said Juliet. She went home and told her father that she would marry Paris. If she had only told her father the truth… well, this would have been a different story.

Lord Capulet was delighted to have his own way, and he began inviting his friends and preparing the wedding feast. Everyone stayed up all night, because there was a great deal to do and very little time to do it. Lord Capulet was eager to see Juliet married because he could see she was very unhappy. Of course, she was really pining for her husband Romeo, but her father thought she was grieving over her cousin Tybalt’s death, and he thought marriage would give her something else to think about.
Early in the morning the nurse came to wake Juliet and dress her for her wedding. But she would not wake, and at last the nurse suddenly cried out:
“Alas! Alas! Help! Help! My lady is dead! Oh, woe is me that I was ever born!”

Lady Capulet came running in, then Lord Capulet, and then Lord Paris, the bridegroom. There lay Juliet, cold and white and lifeless, and all their weeping could not wake her. So that day there was a burial instead of a wedding. Meanwhile Friar Laurence had sent a messenger to Mantua with a letter telling Romeo all of this. Everything would have been well, but the messenger was held up and could not go.

But bad news travels fast. Romeo’s servant knew about the marriage but not about Juliet’s pretended death. He heard about her funeral and rushed off to Mantua to tell Romeo that his young wife was dead and lay in her grave.
“Is it true?” cried Romeo, heartbroken. “Then I will lie by Juliet’s side tonight.”

He bought a poison and went straight back to Verona, then hurried to the tomb where Juliet lay. It was not a grave but a vault. He broke the door open and was about to go down the stone steps into the vault where all the dead Capulets lay, when a voice behind him called out for him to stop.
The voice belonged to Count Paris, the man who was to have married Juliet that very day.
“Vile Montagu! How dare you come here to disturb the dead bodies of the Capulets?” cried Paris.
Poor Romeo, half mad with grief, still tried to answer him gently.
“You were warned,” said Paris, “that if you came back to Verona, you would have to die.”
“I must, indeed,” said Romeo. “I came for nothing else. Good, gentle youth, leave me! Oh, go, before I hurt you! I love you more than myself. Go, leave me here—”
Paris answered, “I defy you, and I am arresting you as a criminal.” In his anger and despair Romeo drew his sword. They fought, and Paris was killed.
As Romeo’s sword pierced him, Paris cried out:
“Oh, I am slain! If you have any mercy, open the tomb and lay me with Juliet!”
And Romeo said, “I will, I promise.”

He carried the dead man into the tomb and laid him beside dear Juliet. Then he knelt next to Juliet, spoke to her, took her in his arms and kissed her cold lips. He believed she was dead, when in fact she was coming closer and closer to the moment of her waking. Then he drank the poison and died beside his sweetheart and wife.
Friar Laurence arrived too late. He saw everything that had happened, and then poor Juliet woke from her sleep to find her husband and her friend both lying dead beside her.

The noise of the fight had drawn other people to the spot, and Friar Laurence heard them coming and ran away, leaving Juliet alone. She saw the cup that had held the poison and understood how it had all happened. No poison was left for her, so she took Romeo’s dagger and drove it through her heart—and falling with her head on her Romeo’s chest, she died. And so ends the story of these faithful and most unhappy lovers.

When the old folks learned the whole truth from Friar Laurence, they were filled with sorrow. They saw now what harm their bitter quarrel had done, and they were sorry for it. At last, over the bodies of their dead children, they joined hands in friendship and forgiveness.

chapters.title: Pericles
paragraphs: Pericles, Prince of Tyre, had the misfortune to make an enemy of Antiochus, the powerful and wicked King of Antioch. The danger was so great that Pericles took the advice of his trusted counselor, Lord Helicanus, and decided to travel the world for a while. He did this even though his father had died and he was now King of Tyre. He sailed for Tarsus and appointed Helicanus to rule as Regent while he was away. It soon became clear that this was a wise way to leave his kingdom.

He had barely set sail when Lord Thaliard arrived from Antioch with orders from his royal master to kill Pericles. The faithful Helicanus soon found out what this wicked lord had come to do, and at once sent messengers to Tarsus to warn the King of the danger hanging over him.

The people of Tarsus were so poor and wretched that Pericles felt he could find no safe refuge there, and he put to sea again. But a terrible storm struck his ship. The good vessel was wrecked, and of everyone on board only Pericles survived. Bruised, soaked and faint, he was flung onto the cruel rocks of the coast of Pentapolis, the land of the good King Simonides. He was worn out and expected nothing but death, and soon. But some fishermen came down to the beach and found him there. They gave him clothes and told him to take heart.
“You shall come home with me,” said one of them, “and we will have meat for holidays, fish for fasting days, and puddings and flapjacks besides, and you will be welcome.”
They told him that the next day many princes and knights were going to the King’s court to compete in jousts and tournaments for the love of his daughter, the beautiful Princess Thaisa.
“If only my fortunes matched my wishes,” said Pericles, “I would like to take part.”

As he spoke, some other fishermen came along, hauling in their net. It was heavy and would not budge for all their efforts, but at last they dragged it in and found a suit of rusty armor inside. When he looked at it, he blessed Fortune for her kindness, because he saw that it was his own, given to him by his dead father. He asked the fishermen to let him have it so he could go to court and join the tournament, and he promised that if his luck ever improved, he would reward them well. The fishermen agreed willingly, and so, fully equipped, Pericles set off for the King’s court in his rusty armor.

In the tournament no one fought as well as Pericles, and he won the wreath of victory, which the lovely Princess herself placed on his brow. Then, at her father’s command, she asked him who he was and where he came from. He answered that he was a knight of Tyre named Pericles, but he did not tell her that he was the King of that country. He knew that if Antiochus ever learned where he was, his life would not be worth a pin.

Even so, Thaisa loved him dearly. The King was so pleased with his courage and graceful manner that he gladly let his daughter have her way when she told him she would marry the stranger knight or die.
And so Pericles became the husband of the lovely lady for whose sake he had competed against the knights who had come in all their splendor to joust and fight for her love.

In the meantime the wicked King Antiochus had died. The people of Tyre had heard no word from their King and urged Lord Helicanus to take the empty throne. All they could get from him was a promise that he would become their King if Pericles had not returned by the end of a year. He also sent messengers far and wide to search for the missing Pericles.

Some of these messengers reached Pentapolis. They found their King there and told him how unhappy his people were at his long absence, and that with Antiochus dead, nothing now kept him from returning to his kingdom. Then Pericles told his wife and his father-in-law who he really was, and they and all of Simonides’ subjects rejoiced to learn that Thaisa’s gallant husband was a King in his own right. So Pericles sailed for his homeland with his dear wife. But once again the sea was cruel to him. Another terrible storm broke out, and at the height of it a servant came to tell him that a little daughter had been born to him. This news would have filled his heart with joy, but the servant added that his wife—his dear, dear Thaisa—was dead.

While Pericles was praying to the gods to be kind to his little baby girl, the sailors came to him. They insisted that the dead Queen had to be thrown overboard, because they believed the storm would never stop as long as a dead body stayed on the ship. So Thaisa was laid in a large chest with spices and jewels, and with a scroll on which the grieving King wrote these lines:

“I make it known here
(If this coffin should wash ashore),
I, King Pericles, have lost
This Queen, worth all earthly wealth.
Whoever finds her, give her a burial;
She was a King’s daughter;
Take this treasure as your payment,
And may the gods repay your kindness!”

Then the chest was thrown into the sea. The waves carried it along and in time washed it ashore at Ephesus, where servants of a lord named Cerimon found it. He ordered it opened at once, and when he saw how lovely Thaisa looked, he doubted that she was dead and immediately set about reviving her. Then a great wonder happened: the woman who had been thrown into the sea for dead came back to life. But she was sure she would never see her husband again, so Thaisa withdrew from the world and became a priestess of the goddess Diana.

While all this was going on, Pericles traveled to Tarsus with his little daughter, whom he named Marina because she had been born at sea. He left her in the care of his old friend, the Governor of Tarsus, and the King sailed on to his own lands.

Now Dionyza, the wife of the Governor of Tarsus, was a jealous and wicked woman. She saw that the young Princess was growing up to be more accomplished and charming than her own daughter, and she decided to have Marina killed. So when Marina was fourteen, Dionyza ordered one of her servants to take her away and murder her. The villain would have done it, but some pirates burst in, seized Marina and carried her off to sea. They took her to Mitylene and sold her as a slave. Yet she was so good, so graceful and so beautiful that she soon won respect there. Lysimachus, the young Governor, fell deeply in love with her and would have married her, but he thought her parents must be too humble for her to be the wife of a man in his high position.

From her servant’s report, the wicked Dionyza believed that Marina really was dead, and she built a monument in her memory. She showed it to King Pericles when, after many years away, he came to see his beloved child. When he heard that she was dead, his grief was terrible to see. He set sail again, put on sackcloth, and swore never to wash his face or cut his hair again. A pavilion was set up on the deck, and he lay there alone, speaking to no one for three months.

At last his ship happened to come into the harbor of Mitylene, and Lysimachus, the Governor, went on board to ask where the vessel had come from. He heard the story of Pericles’ sorrow and silence and thought of Marina. He believed she could rouse the King from his stupor, so he sent for her and told her to do everything she could to make the King speak, promising her any reward she wished if she succeeded. Marina gladly agreed. She sent the others away, sat down and sang to her poor grief-stricken father, but sweet as her voice was, he gave no sign. So after a while she spoke to him and told him that her own sorrow might be as great as his, for although she was a slave, she came from ancestors who were the equals of mighty kings.

Something in her voice and her story touched the King’s heart. He looked up at her, and as he looked, he saw with wonder how much she resembled his lost wife. A great hope rose in his heart, and he asked her to tell her story.

Then, interrupted often by the King’s questions, she told him who she was and how she had escaped from the cruel Dionyza. Pericles knew then that she was truly his daughter. He kissed her over and over, crying that the great seas of his joy were drowning him in their sweetness. “Bring me my robes,” he said. “O Heaven, bless my girl!”
Then he heard the sound of heavenly music, though no one else could hear it, and as he fell asleep he saw the goddess Diana in a vision.
“Go,” she said to him, “to my temple at Ephesus, and when my maiden priestesses have gathered, tell them how you lost your wife at sea.”

Pericles obeyed the goddess and told his tale before her altar. He had barely finished when the chief priestess cried out, “You are—you are—O royal Pericles!” and fell fainting to the ground. When she came to herself, she spoke to him again: “O my lord, are you not Pericles?” “The voice of dead Thaisa!” exclaimed the King in wonder. “I am that Thaisa,” she said, and as he looked at her, he saw that she spoke the plain truth.

So after long and bitter suffering, Pericles and Thaisa found happiness again, and in the joy of their reunion they forgot the pain of the past. Marina, too, was given great happiness, and not only in being restored to her dear parents: she married Lysimachus and became a princess in the land where she had been sold as a slave.

chapters.title: Hamlet
paragraphs: Hamlet was the King of Denmark’s only son. He dearly loved both his father and his mother, and he was happy in the affection of a gentle young woman named Ophelia, whose father, Polonius, served the King as Chamberlain.

While Hamlet was away studying at Wittenberg, his father died. Young Hamlet hurried home in deep grief and was told that a serpent had stung the King and killed him. The young Prince had loved his father so tenderly that you can imagine how he felt when he learned that the Queen, less than a month after the King’s burial, had decided to marry again—and to marry the dead King’s brother.
Hamlet refused to give up his mourning for the wedding.
“It is not only the black clothes I wear,” he said, “that prove my loss. I wear mourning in my heart for my dead father. His son, at least, remembers him and still grieves.”
Then Claudius, the King’s brother, answered him: “Your grief is unreasonable. Naturally you must mourn the loss of your father, but—”
“Ah,” said Hamlet bitterly, “I cannot forget the people I love in one short month.”
With that, the Queen and Claudius went off to enjoy their wedding festivities, forgetting the poor good King who had treated them both so kindly.

Left alone, Hamlet began to wonder and to ask himself what he ought to do. He could not believe the story of the snake bite. It seemed far too plain to him that the wicked Claudius had killed the King in order to get the crown and marry the Queen. Yet he had no proof, and so he could not accuse Claudius.
While he was thinking this over, Horatio, a fellow student from Wittenberg, arrived.
“Why have you come?” Hamlet asked, after he had given his friend a warm welcome.
“I came, my lord, to see your father’s funeral.”
“I think you came to see my mother’s wedding,” said Hamlet bitterly. “My father! We shall never see his like again.”
“My lord,” Horatio replied, “I believe I saw him last night.”

Then, while Hamlet listened in surprise, Horatio explained how he and two gentlemen of the guard had seen the King’s ghost on the castle walls. Hamlet went there that night, and sure enough, at midnight, the ghost of the King appeared on the walls in the chill moonlight, wearing the armor he used to wear. Hamlet was a brave young man. Instead of running from the ghost, he spoke to it, and when it beckoned, he followed it to a quiet place. There the ghost told him that what he had suspected was true. The wicked Claudius had killed his good brother the King by pouring poison into his ear while he slept in his orchard one afternoon.
“And you,” said the ghost, “must take revenge for this foul murder—on my wicked brother. But leave the Queen alone—I have loved her, and she is your mother. Remember me.”
Then, as morning drew near, the ghost vanished.
“Now,” said Hamlet, “nothing is left but revenge. Remember you—I will remember nothing else—books, pleasure, youth—let it all go—and only your commands will live in my mind.”

So when his friends came back, he made them swear to keep the ghost a secret. Then he left the walls, now gray with dawn mixed with moonlight, and went in to think about how best to avenge his murdered father.

The shock of seeing and hearing his father’s ghost left him almost mad. He was afraid his uncle might notice that he was not himself, so he decided to hide his wild longing for revenge behind a pretended madness in everything else.

And when he met Ophelia, who loved him, and to whom he had given gifts and letters and many loving words, he acted so wildly toward her that she could only think he was mad. She loved him so much that she could not believe he would be so cruel unless he were truly out of his mind. So she told her father and showed him a pretty letter from Hamlet. The letter held a good deal of foolishness, and this pretty verse—
From then on, everyone believed that love was the cause of Hamlet’s apparent madness.

Poor Hamlet was very unhappy. He longed to obey his father’s ghost, yet he was too gentle and kind to want to kill another man, even his father’s murderer. And sometimes he wondered whether the ghost had spoken truly after all.

Around this time a troupe of actors came to the Court, and Hamlet asked them to perform a certain play for the King and Queen. The play told the story of a man who was murdered in his garden by a close relative, who then married the dead man’s widow.

You can imagine how the wicked King felt as he sat on his throne, with the Queen beside him and the whole Court around him, and watched the very crime he had committed being acted out on the stage. When the murderer in the play poured poison into the ear of the sleeping man, Claudius suddenly jumped to his feet and stumbled out of the room, with the Queen and others following him.
Then Hamlet said to his friends—
“Now I am certain the ghost told the truth. If Claudius were not guilty of this murder, he could not have been so shaken at seeing it in a play.”

Next, at the King’s request, the Queen sent for Hamlet to scold him for how he had behaved during the play and for other things. Claudius wanted to know exactly what was said, so he told old Polonius to hide behind the wall hangings in the Queen’s room. As they talked, the Queen grew frightened by Hamlet’s rough, strange words and cried out for help, and Polonius cried out too from behind the curtain. Hamlet, thinking the King was hiding there, thrust his sword through the hangings and killed, not the King, but poor old Polonius.
So now Hamlet had offended both his uncle and his mother, and by bad luck had killed the father of the girl he truly loved.
“Oh, what a rash and bloody thing you have done!” cried the Queen.

Hamlet answered bitterly, “Nearly as bad as murdering a king and marrying his brother.” Then he laid out all his thoughts to the Queen and told her how he knew of the murder. He begged her, at the very least, to show no more friendship or kindness to the vile Claudius, who had killed the good King. As they spoke, the King’s ghost appeared to Hamlet once more, though the Queen could not see it. When the ghost was gone, they parted.

When the Queen told Claudius what had happened and that Polonius was dead, he said, “This proves that Hamlet is mad, and now that he has killed the Chancellor, we must carry out our plan for his own safety and send him away to England.”

So Hamlet was sent off in the care of two courtiers who served the King. They carried letters to the English Court demanding that Hamlet be put to death. But Hamlet was clever enough to get hold of these letters and replace them with others, naming the two courtiers who were so eager to betray him. Then, while the ship was sailing to England, Hamlet escaped aboard a pirate ship, and the two wicked courtiers left him to his fate and sailed on to meet their own.

Hamlet hurried home, but meanwhile something dreadful had happened. Poor pretty Ophelia, having lost both her lover and her father, had lost her wits as well. She wandered sadly and madly about the Court with straws, weeds and flowers in her hair, singing odd scraps of songs and saying poor, foolish, pretty things that had no real meaning in them. One day she came to a stream where willows grew and tried to hang a flowery garland on a willow branch. She fell into the water with all her flowers, and so she died.
Hamlet had loved her, though his plan of pretending to be mad had made him hide it. When he came back, he found the King, the Queen and the Court weeping at the funeral of his dear love and lady.

Ophelia’s brother, Laertes, had also just arrived at Court to demand justice for the death of his father, old Polonius. Now, wild with grief, he leaped into his sister’s grave to hold her in his arms one more time.
“I loved her more than forty thousand brothers could,” cried Hamlet, and he leaped into the grave after Laertes, and they fought until they were pulled apart.
Afterward Hamlet begged Laertes to forgive him.
“I could not bear it,” he said, “that anyone, even a brother, should seem to love her more than I did.”

But the wicked Claudius refused to let the two of them make peace. He told Laertes that Hamlet was the one who had killed old Polonius, and between them they hatched a plan to murder Hamlet by treachery.

Laertes challenged Hamlet to a fencing match, with the whole Court watching. Hamlet was given the blunt foil that is always used in fencing, but Laertes had secretly prepared a sharp sword with a poisoned tip. The wicked King had also set out a bowl of poisoned wine, which he meant to hand to poor Hamlet when the sword play made him hot and he asked for a drink.

So Laertes and Hamlet fought, and after some fencing Laertes gave Hamlet a sharp thrust with his sword. Hamlet was angry at this treachery, since they had been fencing as in play and not as men fight in earnest. He grappled with Laertes, and both of them dropped their swords. When they picked them up again, Hamlet had, without noticing, swapped his own blunt sword for Laertes’ sharp, poisoned one. With a single thrust of it he pierced Laertes, who fell dead by his own treachery.
Just then the Queen screamed, “The drink, the drink! Oh, my dear Hamlet! I am poisoned!”
She had drunk from the poisoned bowl that the King had prepared for Hamlet, and the King, wicked as he was, saw the Queen, whom he truly loved, fall dead because of what he had done.

Ophelia was dead now, and so were Polonius, the Queen, Laertes and the two courtiers who had been sent to England. Only then did Hamlet find the courage to carry out the ghost’s command and avenge his father’s murder. Had he steeled himself to do it long before, none of these people would have died, and the only one to suffer would have been the wicked King, who well deserved his death.
At last Hamlet’s heart was strong enough to do what he ought, and he turned the poisoned sword on the false King.
“Then, venom, do your work!” he cried, and the King died.

So in the end Hamlet kept the promise he had made to his father. Now that everything was finished, he died himself. Those standing near watched him die with prayers and tears, for his friends and his people loved him with all their hearts. And so ends the tragic tale of Hamlet, Prince of Denmark.

chapters.title: Cymbeline
paragraphs: Cymbeline was the King of Britain, and he had three children. Both of his sons were stolen away when they were very small, which left him with only one daughter, Imogen. The King married again. He raised Leonatus, the son of a dear friend, to be Imogen’s playmate, and when Leonatus was old enough, Imogen secretly married him. This made the King and the Queen very angry, and to punish Leonatus the King banished him from Britain.

Poor Imogen was nearly heartbroken at parting from Leonatus, and he was no less unhappy. They were not only lovers and husband and wife; they had also been friends and companions since they were very small children. With many tears and kisses they said goodbye. They promised never to forget each other and never to love anyone else as long as they lived.
“This diamond belonged to my mother, my love,” said Imogen. “Take it, my heart, and keep it as long as you still love me.”
“Sweetest and fairest,” Leonatus answered, “put on this bracelet, and wear it for love of me.”
“Oh!” cried Imogen, weeping. “When will we meet again?”
They were still clinging to each other when the King walked in, and Leonatus was forced to go without another word of farewell.

Leonatus arrived in Rome and lodged with an old friend of his father’s. By day he thought of his dear Imogen, and at night he dreamed of her. One day at a feast, some Italian and French noblemen began to talk about their sweethearts, each swearing that his lady was the most faithful, honorable and beautiful in the world. A Frenchman then reminded Leonatus of his many declarations that his wife Imogen was lovelier, wiser and more constant than any lady in France.
“I still say so,” said Leonatus.
“She is not so good that she could not be false,” said Iachimo, one of the Italian nobles.
“She would never be false,” said Leonatus.
“I will bet you,” said Iachimo, “that if I travel to Britain, I can talk your wife into doing anything I please, even against your wishes.”

“You will never do that,” said Leonatus. “I bet this ring on my finger”—which was the very ring Imogen had given him when they parted—“that my wife will keep every vow she made to me, and that you will never persuade her to break one.”

So Iachimo staked half his estate against the ring on Leonatus’s finger and left immediately for Britain, with a letter of introduction to Leonatus’s wife. On his arrival he was received with every courtesy, but he had not given up on winning his bet.

He told Imogen that her husband no longer cared for her, and added many cruel lies about him. Imogen listened at first, but soon she saw what a wicked man Iachimo was and commanded him to leave. At that he said—

“Forgive me, fair lady. Everything I have said is untrue. I told you these things only to see whether you would believe me, or whether you could be trusted as fully as your husband thinks. Will you forgive me?”
“I forgive you freely,” said Imogen.
“Then,” Iachimo went on, “you might prove it by keeping safe a trunk full of jewels that your husband, some other gentlemen and I have bought together as a gift for the Emperor of Rome.”
“Gladly,” said Imogen. “I would do anything for my husband and for a friend of my husband’s. Have the jewels sent to my room, and I will take care of them.”
“It is only for one night,” said Iachimo, “for I leave Britain again tomorrow.”

The trunk was carried into Imogen’s room, and that night she went to bed and slept. Once she was deeply asleep, the lid of the trunk lifted and a man climbed out. It was Iachimo. His tale about the jewels was as false as everything else he had said; he had wanted only to get into her room and win his wicked bet. He looked around and studied the furnishings. Then he crept to the bedside where Imogen lay sleeping and slipped from her arm the gold bracelet her husband had given her at their parting. He crept back into the trunk, and the next morning he sailed for Rome.
When he met Leonatus, he said—

“I have been to Britain and I have won the bet, because your wife no longer thinks of you. She stayed up talking with me for a whole night in her room, which is hung with tapestry and has a carved chimney-piece and silver andirons shaped like two winking Cupids.”
“I don’t believe she has forgotten me, and I don’t believe she spent a night talking with you in her room. The servants must have told you what it looks like.”

“Ah,” said Iachimo, “but she gave me this bracelet. She took it from her arm. I can see her still. The charm of her gesture was worth more than the gift, and yet it made the gift richer. She gave it to me and said she had once prized it.”
“Take the ring,” cried Leonatus. “You have won, and you might have won my life as well, for I care nothing for it now that I know my lady has forgotten me.”

Raging, he wrote to Pisanio, his old servant in Britain, and commanded him to lead Imogen to Milford Haven and kill her there, because she had forgotten him and given away his present. In the same hour he wrote a letter to Imogen herself, telling her to travel with his old servant Pisanio to Milford Haven, where he, her husband, would be waiting to meet her.

When Pisanio received this letter, he was too good a man to carry out its orders and too wise to ignore them completely. So he gave Imogen the letter from her husband and set out with her for Milford Haven. Before he left, the wicked Queen gave him a drink which, she said, would be useful in illness. She hoped he would give it to Imogen and that Imogen would die, so that the Queen’s own son could become King. The Queen believed the drink was poison, but in truth it was only a sleeping potion.
As Pisanio and Imogen drew near Milford Haven, he revealed to her what her husband’s letter to him had really said.
“I must go on to Rome and see him myself,” said Imogen.
Then Pisanio helped her put on boy’s clothes and sent her on her way, and he went back to the Court. Before he left, he gave her the drink he had received from the Queen.

Imogen went on, growing wearier and wearier, until she came to a cave. It seemed that someone lived there, but nobody was at home. She was almost faint with hunger, so she went in and ate some food she found, and she had barely finished when an old man and two boys walked into the cave. She was very frightened, for she thought they would be angry that she had taken their food, although she had meant to leave money for it on the table. To her surprise, though, they greeted her warmly. She looked very pretty in her boy’s clothes, and she had a good face as well as a pretty one.

“You shall be our brother,” both boys told her, and so she stayed on, helping them cook and keeping the cave comfortable. But one day Bellarius, the old man, went hunting with the two boys, and Imogen, who was feeling unwell, decided to try the medicine Pisanio had given her. The moment she swallowed it she lay like a corpse. When Bellarius and the boys came home from the hunt, they believed she was dead. Weeping, and singing funeral songs, they carried her out and laid her in the woods under a covering of flowers.

They sang sweet songs to her and scattered flowers over her—pale primroses, the azure harebell, eglantine and furry moss—and then went away sorrowful. As soon as they were gone, Imogen woke up. She did not know how she had come there or where she was, and she went wandering through the woods.

While Imogen had been living in the cave, the Romans had decided to attack Britain, and their army had crossed the sea. With them came Leonatus, who had grown sorry for his wickedness toward Imogen and so had returned, not to fight for the Romans against Britain, but to fight with the Britons against Rome. As Imogen wandered alone, she met Lucius, the Roman general, and entered his service as his page.

A battle was fought between the Romans and the Britons. Bellarius and his two boys fought for their native land, with Leonatus beside them, dressed as a British peasant. The Romans had captured Cymbeline, but old Bellarius, his sons and Leonatus bravely freed the King. The Britons then won the day. Among the prisoners led before the King were Lucius, Imogen, Iachimo, and Leonatus, who had put on a Roman soldier’s uniform. Ever since he had cruelly ordered his wife’s murder, he had been sick of living, and he hoped to be executed as a Roman soldier.
When they were brought before the King, Lucius spoke up—

“A Roman with a Roman’s heart can suffer,” he said. “If I must die, so be it. This one thing only I ask: let my boy, a Briton born, be ransomed. No master ever had a page so kind, so dutiful, so diligent and true. He has done no harm to any Briton, though he has served a Roman. Save him, sir.”
Cymbeline looked at the page, who was really his own daughter Imogen in disguise. He did not know her, yet he felt such warmth toward the boy that he not only spared his life but said—
“Whatever favor he asks of me, he shall have, even if he asks for a prisoner, the noblest we have taken.”
Imogen answered, “The favor I ask is that this gentleman tell us who gave him the ring he is wearing,” and she pointed at Iachimo.
“Speak,” said Cymbeline. “Where did you get that diamond?”

Then Iachimo confessed the whole truth about his wicked trick. At this Leonatus could no longer hold himself back. He forgot all about his disguise and stepped forward, cursing his own foolishness for believing Iachimo’s lies, and calling out again and again to the wife he thought was dead.
“Oh, Imogen, my love, my life!” he cried. “Oh, Imogen!”
Imogen forgot that she was in disguise and cried out, “Peace, my lord—here, here!”
Leonatus turned to strike the pushy page who dared to break in on his deep grief, and then he saw that it was his wife Imogen. They threw themselves into each other’s arms.

The King was overjoyed to have his dear daughter back, and thankful to the man who had saved him (who turned out to be Leonatus). He gave their marriage his blessing, and then he turned to Bellarius and the two boys. Now Bellarius spoke—

“I am your old servant Bellarius. You accused me of treason when I had been nothing but loyal to you, and being doubted made me disloyal. So I stole your two sons, and look—here they are!” And he led the two boys forward. They had sworn to be brothers to Imogen when they took her for a boy like themselves.
The wicked Queen had died of some of her own poisons, and the King lived on to a happy old age with his three children around him.
So the wicked were punished, and the good and honest lived happily ever after. May the wicked always suffer in that way, and may honest people prosper until the end of the world.

chapters.title: Macbeth
paragraphs: If you ask someone to tell the story of Macbeth, he has two stories to choose from. One is about a man named Macbeth who won the throne of Scotland by a crime in the year of our Lord 1039, and who, on the whole, ruled fairly and well for fifteen years or more. That story belongs to Scottish history. The other story comes from a place called Imagination. It is dark and wonderful, and you shall hear it now.

A year or two before Edward the Confessor became King of England, two generals named Macbeth and Banquo won a battle in Scotland against a Norwegian King. After the battle the two generals walked together toward Forres, in Elginshire, where Duncan, King of Scotland, was waiting for them.
As they crossed a lonely heath, they saw three bearded women. The women were sisters, and they stood hand in hand, withered-looking and wild in their dress.
“Speak! Who are you?” demanded Macbeth.
“Hail, Macbeth, chieftain of Glamis,” said the first woman.
“Hail, Macbeth, chieftain of Cawdor,” said the second woman.
“Hail, Macbeth, who will be King,” said the third woman.
Then Banquo asked, “What about me?” and the third woman answered, “You will be the father of kings.”
“Tell me more,” said Macbeth. “My father’s death made me chieftain of Glamis. But the chieftain of Cawdor is still living, and so are the King and all his children. Speak, I command you!”
The women answered only by vanishing, as if they had suddenly melted into the air.

Banquo and Macbeth now understood that they had been speaking to witches, and they were talking over the prophecies when two nobles came up to them. One of them thanked Macbeth in the King’s name for his services in the war, and the other said, “He told me to call you chieftain of Cawdor.”

Macbeth then learned that the man who had held that title until yesterday was to be put to death for treason, and he could not stop himself from thinking, “The third witch called me, ‘King that will be.’”
“Banquo,” he said, “you see that the witches told the truth about me. So don’t you believe that your child and grandchild will be kings?”

Banquo frowned. Duncan had two sons, Malcolm and Donalbain, and Banquo thought it disloyal to hope that his own son Fleance would rule Scotland. He told Macbeth that the witches might have meant to lure them both into wickedness with their promises about the throne. Macbeth, however, found the prophecy that he would be King far too pleasing to keep to himself, and he told his wife about it in a letter.

Lady Macbeth’s grandfather had been a King of Scotland, killed while defending his crown against the King who ruled before Duncan, and that King had also ordered the death of her only brother. Whenever she looked at Duncan, she remembered those bitter wrongs. Her husband had royal blood too, and as soon as she read his letter, she was determined to make him King.
When a messenger came to tell her that Duncan would spend a night in Macbeth’s castle, she braced herself to do a truly shameful thing.

As soon as she saw Macbeth, she told him that Duncan must have a morning without a sun. She meant that Duncan must die, and that the dead cannot see. “We will talk more of this,” said Macbeth uneasily, and that night, his mind full of Duncan’s kind words, he would gladly have spared his guest.
“Would you rather live as a coward?” demanded Lady Macbeth, who seems to have believed that goodness and cowardice were the same thing.
“I dare do everything that suits a man,” replied Macbeth. “Anyone who dares to do more is no man.”
“Then why did you write me that letter?” she asked fiercely. With bitter words she pushed him on to murder, and with clever words she showed him how to do it.

After supper Duncan went to bed, and two grooms were posted as guards at his bedroom door. Lady Macbeth made them drink wine until they were stupefied. Then she took their daggers, and she would have killed the King herself if his sleeping face had not looked like her father’s.

Macbeth came in afterward and found the daggers lying beside the grooms. Soon he appeared before his wife with bloody hands, saying, “I thought I heard a voice cry, ‘Sleep no more! Macbeth destroys the sleeping.’”
“Go wash your hands,” she said. “Why didn’t you leave the daggers beside the grooms? Take them back, and smear the grooms with blood.”
“I dare not,” said Macbeth.
His wife did dare. She came back to him with hands as red as his own, but, she told him proudly, with a heart that was not so white, for she despised his fear.

Now the murderers heard someone knocking, and Macbeth wished the sound could wake the dead. It was Macduff, chieftain of Fife, whom Duncan had asked to come early. Macbeth let him in and pointed out the door to the King’s chamber.
Macduff walked in, then rushed out again, crying, “O horror! horror! horror!”

Macbeth acted as horror-stricken as Macduff. He pretended he could not bear to see Duncan’s murderers alive, and he killed the two grooms with their own daggers before they could declare their innocence.

These murders did not cry out to be found, and Macbeth was crowned at Scone. One of Duncan’s sons fled to Ireland, the other to England. Macbeth was King. But he was not content. The prophecy about Banquo weighed on his mind. If Fleance were to rule, a son of Macbeth would not. So Macbeth decided to murder both Banquo and his son. He hired two ruffians, who killed Banquo one night as he rode with Fleance to a banquet that Macbeth was giving for his nobles. Fleance got away.

Meanwhile Macbeth and his Queen welcomed their guests very graciously, and he spoke a wish for them that people have repeated thousands of times since his day: “Now may good digestion wait on appetite, and health on both.”
“We beg Your Majesty to sit with us,” said Lennox, a Scottish noble. But before Macbeth could answer, the ghost of Banquo came into the banqueting hall and sat down in Macbeth’s place.

Macbeth did not notice the ghost. He remarked that if Banquo were here, he could say that he had gathered under his roof the finest knights in Scotland. Macduff, however, had bluntly refused his invitation.
Once more the King was urged to take a seat, and Lennox, who could not see Banquo’s ghost, pointed out the chair where it sat.
But Macbeth, who had a seer’s eyes, did see the ghost. To him it looked like a shape made of mist and blood, and he cried out wildly, “Which of you did this?”
Still no one saw the ghost but him, and Macbeth said to the ghost, “You cannot say I did it.”
The ghost slid away, and Macbeth had the nerve to raise a glass of wine “to the joy of everyone at this table, and to our dear friend Banquo, whom we miss.”
They drank the toast, and at that moment Banquo’s ghost walked in a second time.
“Go away!” cried Macbeth. “You have no sense, no mind! Hide in the earth, you horrible shadow.”
Once again no one saw the ghost but him.
“What is it Your Majesty sees?” asked one of the nobles.
The Queen did not dare let anyone answer that question. She hurriedly begged her guests to leave a sick man, who was likely to get worse if he had to talk.
Macbeth, however, was well enough the next day to go and speak with the witches, whose prophecies had corrupted him so badly.
He found them in a cave on a stormy day. They were circling a cauldron in which bits of many strange and horrible creatures were boiling, and they knew he was coming before he arrived.
“Answer what I ask you,” said the King.
“Would you rather hear it from us or from our masters?” the first witch asked.
“Call them,” answered Macbeth.
At that the witches poured blood into the cauldron and grease into the flame that licked at it, and a head wearing a helmet rose up with its visor closed, so that Macbeth could see only its eyes.

He was speaking to the head when the first witch said gravely, “He knows your thought,” and a voice in the head said, “Macbeth, beware Macduff, the chieftain of Fife.” Then the head sank back into the cauldron until it was gone.
“Just one word more,” pleaded Macbeth.
“He will not be commanded,” said the first witch. Then a crowned child rose from the cauldron, holding a tree in his hand. The child said—

“Macbeth cannot be conquered until
Birnam Wood climbs up Dunsinane Hill.”
“That can never happen,” said Macbeth. Then he asked whether any of Banquo’s family would ever rule Scotland.

The cauldron sank into the ground. Music was heard, and a procession of phantom kings passed before Macbeth, with Banquo’s ghost walking behind them. In every king Macbeth saw a likeness to Banquo, and he counted eight kings.
Then suddenly he was left alone.

Next he sent murderers to Macduff’s castle. They did not find Macduff, and they asked Lady Macduff where he was. She gave them a stinging answer, and the man who questioned her called Macduff a traitor. “You lie!” shouted Macduff’s little son. He was stabbed at once, and with his last breath he begged his mother to run. The murderers did not leave the castle while anyone in it was still alive.

Macduff was in England, together with Malcolm, hearing a doctor describe the cures Edward the Confessor had worked, when his friend Ross arrived with the news that Macduff’s wife and children were gone. Ross hardly dared to say it at first, since the truth would turn Macduff’s warm interest in the sick who were healed by a king’s goodness into sorrow and hatred. But then Malcolm announced that England was sending an army to Scotland against Macbeth, and Ross burst out with his news. Macduff cried, “All dead, you say? All my pretty ones and their mother? Did you say all?”

His only sad hope now was revenge. But if he could have looked into Macbeth’s castle on Dunsinane Hill, he would have seen a force more solemn than revenge at work. Retribution was at work, for Lady Macbeth had gone mad. She walked in her sleep through ghastly dreams. She would wash her hands for a quarter of an hour at a time, yet after all that washing she still saw a red spot of blood on her skin. It was pitiful to hear her cry that all the perfumes of Arabia could not make her little hand smell sweet.

“Can you not heal a diseased mind?” Macbeth asked the doctor, but the doctor replied that his patient would have to heal her own mind. This answer made Macbeth scorn medicine. “Throw medicine to the dogs,” he said. “I want none of it.”

One day he heard women crying out. An officer came to him and told him, “Your Majesty, the Queen is dead.” “Out, brief candle,” Macbeth muttered, meaning that life was like a candle that a puff of wind can blow out. He shed no tears; death was too familiar to him now.

Before long a messenger came and said he had seen Birnam Wood moving toward them. Macbeth called him a liar and a slave and swore to hang him if he was wrong. “And if you are right, you may hang me,” he said.

Looking out from the turret windows of Dunsinane Castle, Macbeth saw that Birnam Wood really did appear to be on the march. Each English soldier carried a branch he had cut from a tree in that wood, and like walking trees they climbed up Dunsinane Hill.

Macbeth still had his courage. He went into battle ready to win or die, and he began by killing the English general’s son in single combat. After that he felt that no man could fight him and live. When Macduff came at him, burning for revenge, Macbeth told him, “Turn back. I have shed too much of your blood already.”
“My voice is in my sword,” replied Macduff. He hacked at Macbeth and ordered him to give up.
“I will not give up!” cried Macbeth, but his final hour had come, and he fell.
Macbeth’s soldiers were already retreating when Macduff walked up to Malcolm, carrying a King’s head by the hair.
“Hail, King!” he said, and the new King looked at the old one.
So Malcolm ruled the kingdom after Macbeth; but in later years it was Banquo’s descendants who became kings.

chapters.title: The Comedy of Errors
paragraphs: AEGEON was a merchant from Syracuse, a seaport on the island of Sicily. He and his wife AEmilia were very happy together until AEgeon’s business manager died and he had to travel alone to Epidamnum, a town on the Adriatic. AEmilia joined him as soon as she could, and after they had been there a while, she gave birth to two baby boys. The two were so exactly alike that even in different clothes they looked identical.

And now you must believe something very strange. At the same inn where these children were born, and on the same day, two baby boys were born to a couple much poorer than AEmilia and AEgeon. These twins’ parents were so poor, in fact, that they sold their babies to the parents of the other twins.
AEmilia was eager to show her children to her friends in Syracuse, and so, in dangerous weather, she and AEgeon and the four babies set sail for home.
They were still far from Syracuse when their ship sprang a leak. The crew all left it together in the only boat, caring little what became of the passengers.

AEmilia tied one of her children to a mast and tied one of the slave-children to him. AEgeon followed her example with the other two children. Then the parents tied themselves to the same masts and hoped to be saved.

Suddenly, though, the ship struck a rock and split in two. AEmilia, with the two children she had tied up, drifted away from AEgeon and the other children. Some people of Epidamnum picked up AEmilia and her charges, but some fishermen of Corinth took the babies from her by force, and she went back to Epidamnum alone and very miserable. Afterward she settled in Ephesus, a famous town in Asia Minor.

AEgeon and the children in his care had been rescued too. Luckier than AEmilia, he got back to Syracuse and raised the two boys there until they were eighteen. He named his own son Antipholus and the slave child Dromio, which, oddly enough, were the very names of the children who had drifted away from him.

When he turned eighteen, the son who had stayed with AEgeon grew restless and longed to search for his brother. AEgeon let him go, along with his servant. From here on, the two young men are called Antipholus of Syracuse and Dromio of Syracuse.

Left on his own, AEgeon found his house too gloomy to live in, and he spent the next five years traveling. While he was away he missed some of the news from Syracuse. Had he heard all of it, he would never have set out for Ephesus.

As it happened, his sad wandering ended in that very city, and he was arrested almost the moment he arrived. He learned that the Duke of Syracuse had treated any Ephesians who fell into his hands so cruelly that the government of Ephesus, in anger, had passed a law. Any Syracusan who came to Ephesus would be put to death or else pay a fine of a thousand pounds. AEgeon was taken before Solinus, Duke of Ephesus, who told him he must die or pay a thousand pounds before the day was over.

You will think fate was at work when I tell you that the children kidnaped by the fishermen of Corinth were now citizens of Ephesus. Duke Menaphon, an uncle of Duke Solinus, had brought them there. From now on I will call them Antipholus of Ephesus and Dromio of Ephesus.

What is more, on the same day AEgeon was arrested, Antipholus of Syracuse arrived in Ephesus. To avoid the penalty, he pretended to come from Epidamnum. He gave his money to his servant, Dromio of Syracuse, and told him to carry it to the Centaur Inn and wait there until he came.

Within ten minutes, in the marketplace, he ran into Dromio of Ephesus, his brother’s slave, and at once took him for his own Dromio. “Why are you back so soon? Where did you leave the money?” asked Antipholus of Syracuse.

This Dromio knew of no money except a sixpence he had been given the Wednesday before and had handed to the saddler. But he did know that his mistress was upset because his master had not come home for dinner, and he asked Antipholus of Syracuse to come at once to a house called The Phoenix. His words made the listener angry, and he would have beaten Dromio if Dromio had not run off. Antipholus of Syracuse then went to The Centaur, found that his gold had been left there safely, and walked out of the inn.

He was strolling around Ephesus when two beautiful ladies waved to him. They were sisters, named Adriana and Luciana. Adriana was the wife of his brother, Antipholus of Ephesus. From the strange story Dromio of Ephesus had told her, she had concluded that her husband liked another woman better than his wife. “Yes, you may look as if you don’t know me,” she said to the man who was really her brother-in-law, “but I remember when no words were sweet unless I spoke them, and no meat tasted good unless I carved it.”
“Are you speaking to me?” said Antipholus of Syracuse stiffly. “I don’t know you.”

“Oh, brother, really,” said Luciana. “You know perfectly well that she sent Dromio to tell you to come to dinner.” Then Adriana said, “Come, come, I have been made a fool of long enough. My runaway husband will dine with me, confess his silly pranks, and be forgiven.”
They were determined ladies, and Antipholus of Syracuse got tired of arguing with them. He followed them meekly to The Phoenix, where a very late “midday” dinner was waiting.

Antipholus of Ephesus and his slave Dromio showed up and demanded to be let in while the others were still at dinner. “Maud, Bridget, Marian, Cecily, Gillian, Ginn!” bellowed Dromio of Ephesus, who had all his fellow servants’ names memorized.
A voice from inside answered, “Fool, dray-horse, coxcomb, idiot!” It was Dromio of Syracuse, insulting his own brother without knowing it.

Master and man did everything they could to get in, short of using a crowbar, and finally gave up and left. But Antipholus of Ephesus was so angry with his wife that he decided to give the gold chain he had promised her to another woman.

Inside The Phoenix, Luciana believed that Antipholus of Syracuse was her sister’s husband. When she was alone with him, she gave a speech in rhyme, trying to make him kinder to Adriana. He answered that he was not married, but that he loved her so much that if Luciana were a mermaid, he would gladly lie out on the sea, if only he could feel her floating golden hair beneath him.
Luciana was shocked and left him. She told Adriana about his love-making, and Adriana said her husband was old and ugly and not fit to be seen or heard, though in secret she was very fond of him.
Soon Antipholus of Syracuse had a visitor: Angelo the goldsmith. Antipholus of Ephesus had ordered from him the chain he had promised his wife and meant to give to another woman.

The goldsmith handed the chain to Antipholus of Syracuse and took his “I did not order it” for a mere joke. The puzzled merchant accepted the chain as cheerfully as he had accepted Adriana’s dinner. He offered to pay, but Angelo foolishly said he would come back later.

As a result, Angelo had no money when a creditor, the sort who puts up with no nonsense, threatened to have him arrested unless he paid his debt right away. The creditor had brought a police officer with him. Angelo was relieved to see Antipholus of Ephesus coming out of the house where he had been eating, since he had been locked out of The Phoenix. How bitterly Angelo was dismayed when Antipholus denied ever receiving the chain! Angelo would have had his own mother sent to prison for saying that, and he had Antipholus of Ephesus taken into custody.

Just then Dromio of Syracuse came up and told the wrong Antipholus that he had put their goods on board ship and that a good wind was blowing. To Antipholus of Ephesus this was plain nonsense. He would gladly have beaten the slave, but he only told him sharply to hurry to Adriana and ask her to send her arrested husband a purse of money, which she would find in his desk.

Adriana was furious with her husband because she thought he had been making love to her sister. Still, she did not stop Luciana from fetching the purse, and she told Dromio of Syracuse to bring his master home at once.

Unfortunately, before Dromio could reach the police station, he met his real master, who had never been arrested and could not make sense of the purse Dromio was holding out. Antipholus of Syracuse was even more surprised when a lady he did not know asked him for a chain he had promised her. She was, of course, the lady Antipholus of Ephesus had dined with while his brother sat in his place at the table. “Get away, you witch!” was the answer she got, to her astonishment.

Meanwhile Antipholus of Ephesus waited in vain for the money that was supposed to free him. He was never an even-tempered man, and he was wild with rage when Dromio of Ephesus, who of course had not been told to fetch a purse, showed up with nothing more useful than a rope. Despite the officer’s protests, he beat the slave in the street. His temper did not improve when Adriana, Luciana, and a doctor arrived, convinced that he was mad and needed his pulse taken. He raged so wildly that men stepped forward to tie him up. But Adriana’s kindness spared him that disgrace. She promised to pay the sum demanded of him and asked the doctor to lead him to The Phoenix.

Angelo’s merchant creditor had been paid, and the two were friends again. They might soon have been seen outside an abbey, chatting about the strange behavior of Antipholus of Ephesus. “Quiet,” the merchant said at last, “I think that’s him.”

It was not. It was Antipholus of Syracuse with his servant Dromio, and he was wearing Angelo’s chain around his neck! The two newly reconciled men fairly pounced on him, demanding to know how he dared deny receiving a chain that he had the nerve to wear. Antipholus of Syracuse lost his temper and drew his sword, and at that moment Adriana and several others appeared. “Stop!” cried the careful wife. “Don’t hurt him; he is mad. Take his sword away. Tie him up—and Dromio too.”
Dromio of Syracuse had no wish to be tied up. “Run, master!” he said. “Get into that abbey, fast, or they’ll rob us!”
So they retreated into the abbey.
Adriana, Luciana, and a crowd stayed outside. Then the Abbess came out and said, “People, why are you gathering here?”
“To take home my poor, deranged husband,” Adriana answered.
Angelo and the merchant commented that this was the first they had heard of his being mad.

Adriana then told the Abbess rather too much about her troubles as a wife. The Abbess came away with the idea that Adriana was a scold, and that if her husband was deranged, he had better not go back to her for now.

So Adriana decided to complain to Duke Solinus. And, lo and behold, a minute later the great man appeared with his officers and two other men. The two were AEgeon and the headsman. The thousand marks had not been found, and AEgeon’s fate looked sealed.

Before the Duke could pass the abbey, Adriana knelt in front of him and told a sad tale of a mad husband who ran about stealing jewelry and drawing his sword. She added that the Abbess refused to let her take him home.
The Duke ordered that the Abbess be sent for. He had barely said the words when a servant from The Phoenix came running to Adriana, with the story that his master had burned off the doctor’s beard.
“Nonsense!” said Adriana. “He’s in the abbey.”
“As sure as I’m alive, I’m telling the truth,” said the servant.

Antipholus of Syracuse had barely come out of the abbey when his brother of Ephesus threw himself down before the Duke, crying, “Justice, most gracious Duke, against that woman!” He pointed at Adriana. “She has treated another man as her husband, in my own house.”
While he was still speaking, AEgeon said, “Unless I am raving, I see my son Antipholus.”

No one noticed AEgeon. Antipholus of Ephesus went on to explain how the doctor, whom he called “a threadbare juggler,” had belonged to a gang that tied him up with his slave Dromio and shoved them into a vault. He had escaped by gnawing through his ropes.

The Duke could not understand how the man now talking to him had also been seen going into the abbey. He was still puzzling over it when AEgeon asked Antipholus of Ephesus whether he was not his son. Antipholus answered, “I never saw my father in my life.” But AEgeon was so fooled by his likeness to the brother he had raised that he said, “You are ashamed to acknowledge me in my misery.”
Soon, though, the Abbess came forward, bringing Antipholus of Syracuse and Dromio of Syracuse.
Then Adriana cried, “I see two husbands, or my eyes are deceiving me!” And Antipholus, spotting his father, said, “You are AEgeon, or his ghost.”
Surprises kept coming that day. The Abbess said, “I will pay that man’s fine and set him free, and I will get back the husband I lost. Speak, AEgeon, for I am your wife, AEmilia.”
The Duke was moved. “He is free, and owes no fine,” he said.

AEgeon and AEmilia were together again, and Adriana and her husband made up. Yet nobody was happier than Antipholus of Syracuse, who stepped up to Luciana in the Duke’s presence and said, “I told you that I loved you. Will you marry me?”
She answered with a look, and so her answer is not written down.
The two Dromios were glad to think they would never be beaten again.

chapters.title: The Merchant of Venice
paragraphs: Antonio was a rich and successful merchant of Venice. His ships sailed on almost every sea, and he did business with Portugal, Mexico, England, and India. He was proud of his wealth but very generous with it, and he loved to use it to help his friends in need. Chief among them was his relation Bassanio.

Now Bassanio, like many another cheerful and dashing gentleman, was careless with money and spent too freely. He had not only used up his fortune but could not pay his creditors, so he went to Antonio for more help.
“Antonio,” he said, “I owe you more than anyone, both in money and in love. I have thought of a plan to pay back everything I owe, if only you will help me.”
“Tell me what you need, and I will see that it is done,” his friend replied.

Then Bassanio said, “In Belmont there is a lady who has been left a rich inheritance. Suitors of great fame come from every corner of the world to court her, not just because she is rich, but because she is beautiful and good as well. When we last met, she looked on me so kindly that I am sure I could win her away from all her other admirers, if only I had the means to travel to Belmont, where she lives.”
“Every bit of my fortune,” said Antonio, “is on the sea, so I have no cash at hand. But happily my credit is good in Venice, and I will borrow whatever you need.”

At this time a rich money-lender named Shylock was living in Venice. Antonio despised and disliked him intensely and treated him with the harshest scorn. He would kick him out over his doorstep like a dog, and he would even spit on him. Shylock put up with all these insults with a patient shrug, but deep in his heart he nursed a longing for revenge on the rich, smug merchant. Antonio wounded his pride and hurt his business as well. “If it weren’t for him,” thought Shylock, “I would be richer by half a million ducats. In the marketplace and everywhere else he can, he attacks the rate of interest I charge, and—worse than that—he lends out money for nothing.”

So when Bassanio came to ask him for a loan of three thousand ducats on Antonio’s behalf, for three months, Shylock hid his hatred. Turning to Antonio, he said—“However harshly you have treated me, I would like to be friends with you and have your love. So I will lend you the money and charge no interest. But, just for fun, you will sign a bond. It will say that if you do not repay me within three months, I will have the right to a pound of your flesh, cut from whatever part of your body I choose.”
“No,” Bassanio cried to his friend, “you will not take such a risk for me.”
“Why, don’t be afraid,” said Antonio. “My ships will be home a month before the deadline. I will sign the bond.”

And so Bassanio was supplied with the means to go to Belmont and woo the lovely Portia. On the very night he set out, the money-lender’s pretty daughter, Jessica, ran away from her father’s house with her lover. She took with her some bags of ducats and precious stones from her father’s hoard. Shylock’s grief and rage were terrible to see, and his love for her turned to hate. “I wish she were dead at my feet, with the jewels in her ear,” he cried. His only comfort now was hearing of the serious losses that had struck Antonio, whose ships had in part been wrecked. “Let him look to his bond,” said Shylock. “Let him look to his bond.”

In the meantime Bassanio had arrived at Belmont and called on the lovely Portia. Just as he had told Antonio, he found that word of her wealth and beauty had brought suitors flocking to her from far and wide. To every one of them Portia gave the same answer. She would accept only a man who promised to follow the rules set out in her father’s will. Those rules scared off many an eager suitor. Anyone who wanted to win Portia’s heart and hand had to guess which of three caskets held her portrait. If he guessed right, Portia would become his bride. If he guessed wrong, he had sworn an oath never to say which casket he had chosen, never to marry, and to leave at once.

The three caskets were made of gold, silver, and lead. The gold one carried this inscription—“Whoever chooses me will gain what many men desire.” The silver one read—“Whoever chooses me will get as much as he deserves.” And on the lead one were these words—“Whoever chooses me must give and risk everything he has.” The Prince of Morocco, who was as brave as he was dark-skinned, was one of the first to face the test. He picked the gold casket, because, he said, neither common lead nor silver could hold her picture. So he chose gold, and inside he found the likeness of what many men desire—death.

Next came the proud Prince of Arragon. “Let me have what I deserve,” he said. “Surely I deserve the lady.” He picked the silver casket, and inside he found a fool’s head. “Is a fool’s head all I deserved?” he cried.

At last Bassanio came forward. Portia would gladly have held him back from choosing, so afraid was she that he would choose wrong, for she loved him dearly, just as he loved her. “But,” said Bassanio, “let me choose right now, because as things are, I am living on the rack.”

Then Portia told her servants to fetch musicians and have them play while her brave lover made his choice. Bassanio took the oath and walked up to the caskets, with the musicians playing softly all the while. “Mere outward show,” he said, “is to be despised. The world is still fooled by decoration, so I want no showy gold or glittering silver. I choose the lead casket, and may joy be the result!” He opened it and found fair Portia’s portrait inside. Then he turned to her and asked whether it was really true that she was his.
“Yes,” said Portia. “I am yours, and so is this house. And along with them I give you this ring, which you must never part with.”
Bassanio said he could hardly speak for joy, but he found the words to swear that as long as he lived he would never part with the ring.

Then all at once his happiness was clouded with grief. Messengers arrived from Venice with news that Antonio was ruined, and that Shylock was asking the Duke to enforce the bond, which gave him the right to a pound of the merchant’s flesh. Portia was as upset as Bassanio to hear that his friend was in danger.
“First,” she said, “take me to church and make me your wife. Then go to Venice right away and help your friend. You will take enough money with you to pay his debt twenty times over.”

But after her new husband had left, Portia followed him. She reached Venice disguised as a lawyer, carrying a letter of introduction from Bellario, a famous lawyer whom the Duke of Venice had called in to settle the legal questions raised by Shylock’s claim to a pound of Antonio’s flesh. When the Court met, Bassanio offered Shylock twice the amount he had lent, if only he would give up his claim. But the money-lender’s only reply was—

“Even if each of six thousand ducats
Were split in six, and every piece a ducat,
I’d take none of it—I will have my bond.”

Now Portia arrived in her disguise, and not even her own husband recognized her. The Duke welcomed her because of the great Bellario’s letter, and left the decision in the case to her. Then, in noble words, she begged Shylock to show mercy. But he would not listen. “I will have the pound of flesh,” he answered.
“What do you have to say?” Portia asked the merchant.
“Very little,” he answered. “I am armed and ready.”
“Antonio’s pound of flesh is yours by the Court’s decree,” Portia told the money-lender.
“Most righteous judge!” cried Shylock. “A sentence! Come, get ready.”
“Wait a moment. The bond gives you a right to Antonio’s flesh, but not to any of his blood. If you shed even one drop of it, the State will seize everything you own. That is the Law.”
Shylock, frightened now, said, “Then I will accept Bassanio’s offer.”

“No,” said Portia sternly. “You get your bond and nothing else. Cut your pound of flesh, but remember that if you cut a bit more or a bit less, even by the weight of a hair, you forfeit your property and your life.”
Shylock was now thoroughly alarmed. “Give me the three thousand ducats I lent him, and let him go.”
Bassanio was ready to pay him, but Portia said, “No! He will have nothing except his bond.”

“You are a foreigner,” she went on, “and you have tried to take the life of a Venetian citizen. Under Venetian law, that means your life and your goods are forfeit. Kneel down, then, and beg the Duke for mercy.”

So the tables were turned, and Shylock would have been shown no mercy at all if not for Antonio. As it turned out, the money-lender lost half his fortune to the State, and had to hand the other half over to his daughter’s husband. With that he had to be satisfied.

Bassanio, grateful to the clever lawyer, was persuaded to give up the ring his wife had given him, the one he had promised never to part with. When he went back to Belmont and confessed this to Portia, she seemed very angry and swore she would not be friends with him until she had her ring again. In the end she told him that she herself, disguised as the lawyer, had saved his friend’s life and taken the ring from him. So Bassanio was forgiven, and he was happier than ever to learn what a rich prize he had won in the lottery of the caskets.

chapters.title: Timon of Athens
paragraphs: Four hundred years before Christ was born, there lived in Athens a man whose generosity was not just great but absurd. He was very rich, yet no fortune on earth could be enough for a man who spent and gave away money the way Timon did. If someone gave Timon a horse, Timon sent back twenty better ones. If someone borrowed money from Timon and offered to pay it back, Timon took offense. If a poet wrote a poem and Timon found time to read it, he was sure to buy it, and a painter only had to hold his canvas up in front of Timon to be paid double its market price.

Flavius, his steward, watched this reckless way of living with dismay. When Timon’s house was full of noisy lords drinking and spilling expensive wine, Flavius would sit down in a cellar and weep. He would say to himself, “There are ten thousand candles burning in this house, and every one of those singers braying in the concert room costs a poor man’s whole year’s income in a night.” And he would remember a terrible remark made by Apemantus, one of his master’s friends: “Oh, what a number of men eat Timon, and Timon does not see them!”
Naturally, Timon was praised a great deal.

A jeweler who sold him a diamond claimed that it was not quite perfect until Timon wore it. “You improve the jewel by wearing it,” he said. Timon gave the diamond to a lord named Sempronius, who exclaimed, “Oh, he is the very soul of generosity.” Another lord, named Lucullus, was given a beautiful horse, and said, “Timon is infinitely dear to me.” Other Athenians paid him compliments just as sweet.
But once Apemantus had heard a few of these speeches, he said, “I’m off to knock out an honest Athenian’s brains.”
“You will die for that,” said Timon.
“Then I will die for no reason at all,” said Apemantus. And that, now you know, is the kind of joke people made four hundred years before Christ.

This Apemantus openly despised the human race, but he did it in a healthy way, because he was not unhappy. In this mixed world, anyone with a wide circle of acquaintances knows someone who speaks bitterly about people without avoiding them, who boasts that no fine speech ever fools him, and who is secretly cheerful and proud of himself. Apemantus was that kind of man.
Timon, as you may be surprised to hear, became far worse than Apemantus after the dawn of a certain day that we call Quarter Day.

Quarter Day is the day the bills come pouring in. On that day the grocer, the butcher, and the baker are all thinking about the people who owe them money, and a wise man has saved enough to be ready for them. Timon had not. And he owed more than money for food. He owed it for jewels, horses, and furniture, and worst of all, he owed it to money-lenders, who expected him to repay twice what he had borrowed.

Quarter Day is when promises to pay are met with scorn, and on that day a large sum was demanded of Timon. “Sell some land,” he told his steward. “You have none left,” came the reply. “Nonsense! I had a hundred thousand acres,” said Timon. “You could have spent the price of the whole world, had you owned it,” said Flavius.

“Then borrow some,” said Timon. “Try Ventidius.” He thought of Ventidius because he had once paid off a creditor of this young man and so gotten him out of prison. Ventidius was rich now, and Timon trusted in his gratitude. But one loan would not be enough, so much did he owe! Servants were sent off to several friends with requests for loans:
