One servant, Flaminius, went to Lucullus. When he was announced, Lucullus said, “A gift, I’ll bet. Last night I dreamed of a silver jug and basin.” Then, changing his tone, he said, “And how is that honorable, openhearted, perfect gentleman, your master, eh?”
“In good health, sir,” replied Flaminius.
“And what have you got under your cloak there?” Lucullus asked cheerfully.
“Truly, sir, nothing but an empty box. On my master’s behalf, I beg you to fill it with money, sir.”

“La! la! la!” said Lucullus, who could not pretend to mean “Ha! ha! ha!” “Your master’s one fault is that he loves giving parties too much. I’ve warned him that it was expensive. Now, look here, Flaminius, you know this is no time to lend money without security. So be a good boy and tell him I wasn’t at home. Here are three solidares for yourself.”
“Go back, wretched money,” cried Flaminius, “to the one who worships you!”
Others among Timon’s friends were tried and found to be stingy. One of them was Sempronius.
“Hmm,” he said to Timon’s servant, “has he asked Ventidius? Ventidius owes him a favor.”
“He refused.”
“Well, have you asked Lucullus?”
“He refused.”

“It’s a poor compliment to come to me last of all,” said Sempronius, putting on a show of anger. “If he had sent to me first, I would gladly have lent him money. But I’m not fool enough to lend him any now.”
“Your lordship makes a fine villain,” said the servant.

When Timon learned how mean his friends were, he used a pause in the storm of his creditors to invite Ventidius and Company to a banquet. Flavius was horrified, but Ventidius and Company were not the least bit ashamed. They gathered at Timon’s house as invited, telling one another that their princely host had only been joking with them.
“I had to put off an important engagement to come here,” said Lucullus, “but who could say no to Timon?”
“It truly grieved me to have no ready money when he asked me for some,” said Sempronius.
“It was the same with me,” chimed in a third lord.
Timon now came in, and his guests competed with one another in apologies and compliments. Inwardly sneering, Timon was gracious to every one of them.
In the banqueting hall stood a table gleaming with covered dishes. Mouths watered. These fair-weather friends loved good food.

“Be seated, worthy friends,” said Timon. Then he prayed aloud to the gods of Greece. “Give each man enough,” he said, “because if you, who are our gods, had to borrow from men, they would stop worshiping you. Let men love the roast more than the host. Let every twenty guests include twenty villains. Bless my friends as much as they have blessed me. Uncover the dishes, you dogs, and lap it up!”
The hungry lords were too astonished by this speech to take offense. They thought Timon must be unwell, and even though he had called them dogs, they uncovered the dishes.
There was nothing in them but warm water.

“May you never see a better feast,” said Timon. “I wash off the flattery you smeared on me, and I sprinkle you with your own villainy.” With these words he threw the water in his guests’ faces and then pelted them with the dishes. Having ended the banquet this way, he went into an outhouse, grabbed a spade, and left Athens forever.
His next home was a cave near the sea.

Of all his friends, the only one who had not refused him help was a handsome soldier named Alcibiades, and Timon had not asked him because Alcibiades had quarreled with the Government of Athens and left the city. The thought that Alcibiades might have proved a true friend did not soften Timon’s bitterness. He was too weak-minded to see that in this mixed world, good is never far from evil. He made up his mind to see nothing better in all mankind than the ingratitude of Ventidius and the meanness of Lucullus.
He turned vegetarian, and as he grubbed in the dirt for his food he talked to himself at endless length.

One day he was digging for roots near the shore when his spade hit gold. A wise man would have made himself rich in no time and gone home to Athens to live comfortably. But the sight of the vein of gold brought Timon no joy, only contempt. “This yellow slave,” he said, “will make and break religions. It will turn black to white and ugly to fair. It will buy murder and bless the cursed.”
While he was still raving, Alcibiades walked up, an enemy of Athens now, with his soldiers and two lovely women who thought of nothing but pleasure.
Timon had been so changed by his bitter thoughts and rough life that at first Alcibiades did not recognize him.
“Who are you?” he asked.
“A beast, like you,” was the answer.

Alcibiades recognized his voice and offered him help and money. But Timon wanted none of it, and began to insult the women. When they learned that he had found a gold mine, though, they cared nothing for his opinion of them, and said, “Give us some gold, good Timon. Have you more?”
Hurling more insults, Timon stuffed their aprons full of gold ore.

“Farewell,” said Alcibiades, who decided that Timon had lost his wits. Then his well-disciplined soldiers walked away from the mine, which could have paid their wages, without taking a thing, and marched toward Athens.
Timon went on digging and cursing, and he pretended to be delighted whenever he dug up a root and found it was not a grape.
Just then Apemantus appeared. “I hear that you are copying me,” said Apemantus. “Only,” said Timon, “because you don’t have a dog I could copy.”
“You are taking revenge on your friends by punishing yourself,” said Apemantus. “That is very foolish, because they are living as comfortably as ever. I’m sorry that a fool should copy me.”
“If I were like you,” said Timon, “I’d throw my life away.”
“You already have,” Apemantus sneered. “Will the cold brook make you a good morning drink, or will an east wind warm your clothes the way a valet would?”

“Be gone!” said Timon. But Apemantus lingered a little longer and told him that he was fond of extremes, which was true. Apemantus even tried a pun, yet there was no real laughter to be had from Timon.
At last they lost their tempers like two schoolboys. Timon said he was sorry to waste a stone by throwing it at Apemantus, who walked off muttering a curse on him.
It turned into something like a reception day for Timon, because as soon as Apemantus was gone, some robbers came to see him. They were after gold.
“That’s asking too much,” said Timon. “I have only water, roots and berries.”
“We’re not birds and pigs,” said one of the robbers.
“No, you are cannibals,” said Timon. “Then take the gold, and may it poison you! From now on, rob each other.”

He spoke to them so terribly that even though they left with their pockets full, they very nearly regretted their trade. The last visitor of that busy day was his faithful steward Flavius. “My dearest master!” he cried.
“Go away! Who are you?” said Timon.
“Have you forgotten me, sir?” Flavius asked sadly.
“I have forgotten all men,” came the answer, “and if you’ll admit that you are a man, then I have forgotten you too.”
“I was your honest servant,” said Flavius.
“Nonsense! I never had an honest man around me,” Timon snapped back.
Flavius started to cry.
“What! Tears?” said Timon. “Then come closer. I will love you because you are a woman, and not like men, who weep only when they are laughing or begging.”

They talked for a while, and then Timon said, “That gold over there is mine. I will make you rich, Flavius, if you promise to live alone and hate mankind. I will make you very rich if you promise to watch the flesh waste off a beggar’s bones before you give him a meal, and to let a debtor die in prison before you pay what he owes.”
Flavius answered only, “Master, let me stay here and comfort you.”
“If you don’t like cursing, leave me,” Timon replied, and he turned his back on Flavius. The steward went sadly back to Athens, for he was too used to obeying to push his help on his sick master.

Flavius had taken nothing, but a rumor spread that his old master had given him a huge lump of gold, and so Timon had still more visitors. They were a painter and a poet, both men he had supported when he was rich.
“Greetings, noble Timon!” said the poet. “We were amazed to hear how your friends abandoned you. No whip is big enough for their backs!”
“We have come,” the painter broke in, “to offer you our services.”
“You have heard that I have gold,” said Timon.
“There was a rumor,” said the painter, turning red, “but my friend and I did not come because of that.”
“Good, honest men!” Timon sneered. “All the same, you will get plenty of gold if you will rid me of two villains.”

“Tell us who they are,” said the two visitors together. “You two!” answered Timon. He gave the painter a whack with a big stick and said, “Put that on your palette and make some money from it.” Then he whacked the poet and said, “Make a poem of that and get paid for it. There’s your gold.”
They hurried away.
Last of all, Timon had a visit from two senators. Athens was now threatened by Alcibiades, and they wanted this embittered nobleman on their side, since his gold might help the enemy.
“Forget the wrongs done to you,” said the first senator. “Athens offers you high honors, so that you can live with dignity.”
“Athens admits that your worth was overlooked, and she wants to make up for it, and more than make up for it, for having forgotten you,” said the second senator.
“Worthy senators,” Timon answered grimly, “I am nearly in tears, you move me so! All I need are the eyes of a woman and the heart of a fool.”

But the senators loved their city. They believed that this embittered man could still save Athens, and they would not argue with him. “Become our captain,” they begged, “and lead Athens against Alcibiades, who means to destroy her.”
“As far as I care, let him destroy the Athenians too,” said Timon. When they saw the wicked despair on his face, they left him.

The senators went back to Athens, and soon after, trumpets sounded outside its walls. The senators stood on the walls and listened to Alcibiades, who told them that wrongdoers should tremble in their easy chairs. They looked at his confident army and were sure that Athens would have to give way if he attacked. So they spoke with the one voice that cuts deeper than arrows.
“The men who built these walls of ours never did you any wrong, Alcibiades,” said the first senator.
“Come inside,” said the second senator, “and put every tenth man to death, if your revenge must have human flesh.”
“Spare the cradle,” said the first senator.
“I ask only for justice,” said Alcibiades. “If you let my army in, I will punish any soldier who breaks your laws with the penalty your own laws set.”

Just then a soldier came up to Alcibiades and said, “My noble general, Timon is dead.” He handed Alcibiades a sheet of wax and said, “He is buried by the sea, on the beach. Over his grave is a stone with letters on it that I cannot read, so I pressed them into wax.”
Alcibiades read this couplet on the sheet of wax—

“Here I lie, Timon, who in life
hated all living men.
Walk by and say the worst you like, but walk on,
and do not linger here.”
“So noble Timon is dead,” said Alcibiades, and he entered Athens carrying an olive branch instead of a sword.

So it was one of Timon’s friends who proved generous in a greater matter than Timon’s own need. Still, Timon’s sorrow and rage are remembered as a warning, so that no other ingratitude may arise to turn love into hate.

chapters.title: Othello
paragraphs: Four hundred years ago in Venice there lived an ensign named Iago, who hated his general, Othello, for not making him a lieutenant. Iago had been strongly recommended, but Othello had chosen Michael Cassio instead, a man whose smooth talk had helped him win the heart of Desdemona. Iago had a friend named Roderigo, who gave him money and believed he could never be happy unless Desdemona became his wife.

Othello was a Moor, with a complexion so dark that his enemies called him a Blackamoor. His life had been hard and full of adventure. He had been defeated in battle and sold as a slave, and he had traveled widely and seen men whose shoulders stood higher than their heads. He was as brave as a lion, and he had one great fault—jealousy. His love was a terrible kind of selfishness. For him, loving a woman meant owning her as completely as he owned something that neither lived nor thought. The story of Othello is a story of jealousy.

One night Iago told Roderigo that Othello had run off with Desdemona without the knowledge of her father, Brabantio. He talked Roderigo into waking Brabantio, and when the senator came out, Iago told him about Desdemona’s elopement in the nastiest way he could. Though he was Othello’s own officer, he called him a thief and a Barbary horse.

Brabantio accused Othello before the Duke of Venice of using witchcraft to charm his daughter. Othello answered that the only witchcraft he had used was his voice, which had told Desdemona about his adventures and narrow escapes. Desdemona was brought into the council chamber, and she explained how she could love Othello in spite of his nearly black face by saying, “I saw Othello’s visage in his mind.”

Othello had married Desdemona, and she was glad to be his wife, so there was nothing more to be said against him. The Duke, besides, wanted him to go to Cyprus and defend it against the Turks. Othello was quite ready to go, and Desdemona, who begged to go with him, was allowed to follow him to Cyprus.

Othello was filled with joy when he landed on the island. Desdemona had arrived ahead of him, with Iago, his wife, and Roderigo. “Oh, my sweet,” he said to her, “I hardly know what to say to you. I am in love with my own happiness.”
Soon word came that the Turkish fleet had been put out of action, and he announced a festival in Cyprus, to last from five o’clock until eleven at night.

Cassio was on duty in the castle from which Othello governed Cyprus, so Iago decided to get the lieutenant drunk. It was not easy, because Cassio knew that wine soon went to his head. But servants brought wine into the room where Cassio was, and Iago sang a drinking song, and so Cassio raised his glass once too often to the health of the general.

When Cassio grew quarrelsome, Iago told Roderigo to say something insulting to him. Cassio beat Roderigo with a stick, and Roderigo ran into the presence of Montano, the former governor. Montano politely stepped in on Roderigo’s behalf, but Cassio answered him so rudely that Montano said, “Come, come, you’re drunk!” Cassio then wounded him, and Iago sent Roderigo out to alarm the town with a cry of mutiny.
The uproar woke Othello, and when he learned what had caused it, he said, “Cassio, I love you, but never again will you be an officer of mine.”

When Cassio and Iago were left alone, the disgraced man moaned about his reputation. Iago said that reputation and humbug were the same thing. “O God,” Cassio cried, not listening to him, “that men should put an enemy in their mouths to steal away their brains!”

Iago advised him to beg Desdemona to ask Othello to forgive him. Cassio liked the advice, and the next morning he made his request to Desdemona in the castle garden. She was kindness itself and said, “Cheer up, Cassio, for I would rather die than give up your cause.”
At that moment Cassio saw Othello coming toward them with Iago, and he hurried away.
Iago said, “I don’t like that.”

“What did you say?” asked Othello, who felt that Iago had meant something unpleasant. But Iago pretended he had said nothing. “Wasn’t that Cassio who just left my wife?” Othello asked. Iago knew perfectly well that it was Cassio, and why he was there, but he said, “I cannot believe it was Cassio who slipped away in such a guilty manner.”

Desdemona told Othello that it was grief and shame that made Cassio shrink from him. She reminded him how Cassio had stood up for him when she was still free of love and had found fault with her Moorish suitor. Othello softened and said, “I will deny you nothing,” but Desdemona told him that what she asked was as much for his own good as eating dinner.
Desdemona went out of the garden, and Iago asked whether Cassio had really known Desdemona before she was married.
“Yes,” said Othello.
“Indeed,” said Iago, as if something that had puzzled him had now become very clear.
“Isn’t he honest?” Othello demanded, and Iago repeated the word as a question, as if he were afraid to say “No.”
“What do you mean?” Othello pressed him.

Here Iago would say only the very opposite of what he had said to Cassio. To Cassio he had called reputation humbug. To Othello he said, “Who steals my purse steals trash, but he who takes my good name from me ruins me.”

At this Othello almost jumped in the air. Iago felt so sure of his jealousy that he dared to warn him against it. It was none other than Iago who spoke of jealousy as “the green-eyed monster which doth mock the meat it feeds on.”
Having given jealousy one blow, Iago went on to feed it, remarking that Desdemona had deceived her father when she eloped with Othello. What he meant was, “If she deceived him, why not you?”

Soon Desdemona returned to tell Othello that dinner was ready. She saw that he was troubled, and he blamed a pain in his forehead. Desdemona then took out a handkerchief that Othello had given her. A prophetess two hundred years old had made it from the silk of sacred silkworms, dyed it in a liquid made from the hearts of maidens, and embroidered it with strawberries. Gentle Desdemona saw in it only something cool and soft for an aching forehead. She knew of no spell on it that would bring ruin to the woman who lost it. “Let me tie it around your head,” she said to Othello. “In an hour you will be well.” But Othello said crossly that it was too small, and let it drop. Then he and Desdemona went in to dinner, and Emilia picked up the handkerchief, which Iago had often told her to steal.
She was examining it when Iago walked in. They exchanged a few words about it, and then he snatched it away from her and ordered her to go.

In the garden Othello joined him, looking hungry for the worst lies Iago could offer. So Iago told him that he had seen Cassio wipe his mouth with a handkerchief, and that since it was spotted with strawberries, he guessed it was the one Othello had given his wife.

The unhappy Moor was driven mad with fury. Iago called on the heavens to witness that from now on his hand, his heart and his brain belonged to Othello. “I take your love,” said Othello. “Within three days let me hear that Cassio is dead.”

Iago’s next step was to drop Desdemona’s handkerchief in Cassio’s room. Cassio found it and knew it was not his own, but the strawberry pattern pleased him, so he gave it to his sweetheart Bianca and asked her to copy it.

Iago’s next move was to get Othello, who had been bullying Desdemona about the handkerchief, to listen in secret to a conversation between Cassio and himself. He meant to talk about Cassio’s sweetheart and let Othello suppose that the lady they spoke of was Desdemona.
“How are you, lieutenant?” Iago asked when Cassio appeared.
“Worse, for being called something I am not,” Cassio answered gloomily.
“Keep pestering Desdemona, and you’ll soon get your rank back,” said Iago. In a voice too low for Othello to hear, he added, “If Bianca could fix the matter, how quickly it would be mended!”

“Alas, poor girl!” said Cassio. “I really think she loves me.” Cassio, the talkative show-off that he was, was drawn on to boast of Bianca’s fondness for him, while Othello, choking with rage, imagined that he was chattering about Desdemona, and thought, “I see your nose, Cassio, but not the dog I shall throw it to.”

Othello was still spying when Bianca came in, boiling with the idea that Cassio, whom she thought of as her property, had asked her to copy the embroidery on a new sweetheart’s handkerchief. She tossed it to him with scornful words, and Cassio left with her.

Othello had seen Bianca, who was lower in rank, and far inferior to Desdemona in beauty and speech, and in spite of himself he began to praise his wife to the villain in front of him. He praised her skill with the needle, her voice that could “sing the savageness out of a bear,” her wit, her sweetness, the fairness of her skin. Each time he praised her, Iago said something that made him remember his anger and speak it out in ugly words, and yet he could not help praising her and saying, “The pity of it, Iago! O Iago, the pity of it, Iago!”
In all of Iago’s villainy there was never a single moment of wavering. If there had been, he might have wavered then.
“Strangle her,” he said, and his wretched dupe answered, “Good, good!”

The two were still talking of murder when Desdemona came in with Lodovico, a relative of her father’s, who carried a letter for Othello from the Duke of Venice. The letter called Othello back from Cyprus and gave the governorship to Cassio.
Unlucky Desdemona seized this unhappy moment to plead once more for Cassio.
“Fire and brimstone!” Othello shouted.
“Perhaps the letter has upset him,” Lodovico explained to Desdemona, and he told her what it said.
“I am glad,” said Desdemona. It was the first bitter word that Othello’s unkindness had forced from her.
“I am glad to see you lose your temper,” said Othello.
“Why, dear Othello?” she asked, with a sting in her voice, and Othello struck her across the face.

Now was the time for Desdemona to save her life by leaving him, but she did not know her danger. She knew only that her love was wounded to the core. “I have not deserved this,” she said, and tears ran slowly down her face.

Lodovico was shocked and disgusted. “My lord,” he said, “no one in Venice would believe this. Make it up to her.” But Othello, like a madman talking in a nightmare, poured out his foul thoughts in ugly words and roared, “Out of my sight!”
“I won’t stay to anger you,” said his wife, but she lingered even as she left, and only when he shouted “Get out!” did she go and leave her husband with his guests.
Othello then asked Lodovico to supper. “You are welcome to Cyprus, sir,” he added. “Goats and monkeys!” And without waiting for any answer, he walked out on the company.
Distinguished visitors hate being made to watch a family quarrel, and they do not enjoy being called goats or monkeys, so Lodovico asked Iago what it all meant.

Iago stayed true to his nature. In a roundabout way he told them that Othello was worse than he appeared, and he advised them to watch how Othello behaved and spare him the pain of answering any more questions.

Then he told Roderigo to kill Cassio. Roderigo was no longer on good terms with his friend. He had handed Iago a great many jewels to give to Desdemona, and nothing had come of it; Desdemona had never seen a single one, because Iago was a thief and had kept them.

Iago soothed him with a lie. When Cassio was leaving Bianca’s house, Roderigo attacked and wounded him, and was wounded in return. Cassio cried out, and Lodovico and a friend came running. Cassio named Roderigo as the man who had attacked him, and Iago, hoping to be rid of a friend who had become a nuisance, called him “Villain!” and stabbed him, though not fatally.

At the Castle, Desdemona was sad and low. She told Emilia she must send her away, because her husband wanted it. “Send me away!” cried Emilia. “It was his wish,” said Desdemona, “and we must not displease him now.”

She sang a song once sung by a girl whose lover had treated her badly, a song about a maiden weeping beside the tree whose branches droop as if it were weeping too. Then she went to bed and fell asleep.

She woke to find her husband’s wild eyes fixed on her. “Have you said your prayers tonight?” he asked. Then he told this innocent, gentle woman to ask God’s forgiveness for any sin that lay on her conscience. “I would not kill your soul,” he said.

He told her that Cassio had confessed. But she knew that Cassio had nothing to confess that touched her, and she said he could say nothing to harm her. Othello answered that Cassio’s mouth had been shut for good.
Desdemona wept then, but Othello, ignoring all her pleading, answered with violent words and pressed his hands on her throat until he had mortally hurt her.
Then Emilia came, her heart heavy with dread, and begged to be let in at the door. Othello unlocked it, and a voice came from the bed, saying, “I die an innocent death.”
“Who did this?” cried Emilia, and the voice said, “No one—I did it myself. Farewell!”
“It was I who killed her,” said Othello.
By that sad bed he poured out his proofs to the people who came running in, Iago among them. But when he spoke of the handkerchief, Emilia told the truth.
And Othello understood. “Are there no stones in heaven except thunderbolts?” he cried, and rushed at Iago, who dealt Emilia her death-blow and ran away.
But Iago was caught and brought back, and the death that came to him later was a release from torture.

They meant to take Othello back to Venice to be tried there, but he escaped them with his sword. “Let me say a word or two before you go,” he told the Venetians in the room. “Speak of me as I was—no better and no worse. Say that I threw away the pearl of pearls, and wept with these hard eyes. And say that once in Aleppo, years ago, I saw a Turk beating a Venetian, and I took him by the throat and struck him like this.”
With his own hand he stabbed himself through the heart, and before he died his lips touched Desdemona’s face with despairing love.

chapters.title: The Taming of the Shrew
paragraphs: In Padua there lived a gentleman named Baptista, who had two lovely daughters. The elder, Katharine, was so cross, bad-tempered and rude that nobody ever dreamed of marrying her. Her sister Bianca, on the other hand, was so sweet, pretty and pleasant in her speech that more than one suitor had asked her father for her hand. But Baptista insisted that the elder daughter must be married first.
So Bianca’s suitors agreed among themselves to find someone who would marry Katharine—and then the father could at least be persuaded to listen to their offers for Bianca.

The man they thought of was a gentleman from Verona named Petruchio. Half as a joke, they asked whether he would marry Katharine, that disagreeable scold. To their great surprise he said yes, she was exactly the wife for him. If Katharine were beautiful and rich, he said, he would soon take it upon himself to make her good-tempered.

Petruchio began by asking Baptista’s permission to court his gentle daughter Katharine, and Baptista had to admit that she was anything but gentle. Just then her music master burst in, complaining that the wicked girl had broken her lute over his head, because he had told her she was playing it wrongly.
“Never mind,” said Petruchio. “I love her better than ever, and I long to talk with her.”
When Katharine came in, he said, “Good morning, Kate—for that, I hear, is your name.”
“You’ve heard only half of it,” said Katharine rudely.

“Oh no,” said Petruchio. “They call you plain Kate, and pretty Kate, and sometimes Kate the shrew. And since I have heard your gentleness praised in every town, and your beauty too, I am asking you to be my wife.”
“Your wife!” cried Kate. “Never!” She hurled some truly nasty remarks at him and, I am sorry to say, topped them off by slapping his face.
“Do that again and I’ll hit you back,” he said calmly. And with many compliments, he went on declaring that he would marry no one but her.
When Baptista came back, he asked at once—
“How are you getting on with my daughter?”
“How could I get on except well?” answered Petruchio. “How else but well?”
“And you, daughter Katharine?” the father went on. “How is it with you?”
“I don’t think,” said Katharine angrily, “that you are acting like a father when you wish me to marry this mad ruffian.”

“Ah,” said Petruchio, “you and everyone else misjudge her. You should see how sweet she is to me when we are alone. Anyway, I’m off to Venice to buy fine things for the wedding—and—kiss me, Kate!—we marry on Sunday.”

At that, Katharine stormed out of the room by one door in a furious temper, and he went out by the other, laughing. Perhaps she fell in love with Petruchio. Perhaps she was only glad to meet a man who was not afraid of her. Perhaps she was flattered that, in spite of her rough words and spiteful treatment, he still wanted her for his wife. Whatever the reason, she did marry him on Sunday, just as he had sworn she would.

To annoy and humble Katharine’s proud, wilful spirit, he arrived late at the wedding, and when he came, he was dressed in such shabby clothes that she was ashamed to be seen with him. His servant was dressed just as shabbily, and the horses they rode made everyone they passed laugh.

After the marriage, when the wedding breakfast should have been served, Petruchio carried his wife off without letting her eat or drink anything. She was his now, he said, and he could do as he liked with her.

He was so violent, and acted through the whole wedding in such a wild and frightening way, that Katharine trembled and went with him. He put her on a lean old horse that stumbled, and they traveled over rough, muddy roads to Petruchio’s house, with him scolding and snarling the whole way.

When she reached her new home she was terribly tired, but Petruchio was determined that she should neither eat nor sleep that night. He had made up his mind to teach his bad-tempered wife a lesson she would never forget.

So he welcomed her to his house kindly enough, but when supper was served he found fault with everything. The meat was burnt, he said, and badly served, and he loved her far too much to let her eat anything but the best. In the end Katharine, worn out from the journey, went to bed without supper. Then her husband, still telling her how much he loved her and how anxious he was that she should sleep well, tore her bed apart and threw the pillows and bedclothes on the floor, so that she could not go to bed at all. All the while he kept growling and scolding at the servants, so that Kate might see how ugly a thing bad temper was.
The next day her food was again criticized and snatched away before she could touch a mouthful, and she felt sick and dizzy from lack of sleep. Then she said to one of the servants—
“Please go and get me something to eat. I don’t care what.”
“How about a calf’s foot?” said the servant.
Katharine said “Yes,” eagerly. But the servant, who was in his master’s secret, said he was afraid it was not good for people with hasty tempers. Would she like tripe instead?
“Bring it to me,” said Katharine.
“I’m afraid that’s bad for hasty people too,” said the servant. “Would you like a dish of beef with mustard?”
“I love it,” said Kate.
“But mustard is too hot.”
“Well then, the beef, and forget the mustard,” cried Katharine, who was growing hungrier and hungrier.
“No,” said the servant. “Either you take the mustard, or there’s no beef for you from me.”
“Then,” cried Katharine, losing patience, “bring both, or one, or whatever you like.”
“Very well, then,” said the servant. “The mustard without the beef!”
Then Katharine realized he was making fun of her, and she slapped him across the face.

Soon after, Petruchio brought her a little food, but she had hardly begun to ease her hunger when he sent for the tailor to show her the new clothes, and the table was cleared away with her still hungry. Katharine loved the pretty gown and cap the tailor had made her. Petruchio, though, picked at every part of them, threw the cap and gown to the floor, and vowed that his dear wife would never wear such silly things.
“But I want them,” cried Katharine. “Every gentlewoman wears caps like these—”

“When you are gentle, you shall have one too,” he answered, “and not before.” He drove the tailor away with angry words, though he privately asked his friend to make sure the man was paid. Then Petruchio said—

“Come, Kate, we’ll go to your father’s just as we are, shabby clothes and all. The sun breaks through the darkest clouds, and honor shines out even from the humblest dress. It’s about seven o’clock now, and we’ll easily arrive in time for dinner.”

“It’s nearly two,” said Kate, but politely enough, for she had come to see that she could not bully her husband the way she had bullied her father and her sister. “It’s nearly two, and it will be suppertime before we get there.”

“It shall be seven,” said Petruchio stubbornly, “before I start. Whatever I say or do or think, you do nothing but contradict me. I won’t go today, and before I do go, it will be whatever time I say it is.”
At last they set out for her father’s house.
“Look at the moon,” he said.
“That’s the sun,” said Katharine, and it truly was.
“I tell you it’s the moon. Contradicting me again! It will be sun or moon or whatever I decide, or else I’m not taking you to your father’s.”

Then Katharine gave in, once and for all. “Whatever you want to call it,” she said, “that is what it is, and so it shall be for Katharine.” And so it was, for from that moment Katharine knew she had met her master, and she never again showed her bad temper to him or to anyone else.

So they went on to Baptista’s house, and when they arrived they found everyone celebrating Bianca’s wedding feast along with that of another newly married couple, Hortensio and his wife. They were made welcome and sat down to the feast, and all was merry except that Hortensio’s wife, seeing Katharine tamed by her husband, thought she could safely say many unpleasant things that she would never have dared say in the old days, when Katharine was free and wilful. But Katharine answered with such spirit and such good sense that she turned the laugh against the new bride.
After dinner, when the ladies had left the room, Baptista joined in a laugh at Petruchio’s expense. “In all seriousness, son Petruchio,” he said, “I fear you have got the worst shrew of all.”

“You are wrong,” said Petruchio. “Let me prove it to you. Each of us will send a message to his wife, asking her to come to him, and the man whose wife comes most willingly will win a wager that we shall agree on.”
The others agreed readily enough, for each thought his own wife the most dutiful, and each felt sure he would win the wager.
They proposed a wager of twenty crowns.
“Twenty crowns,” said Petruchio. “I would risk that much on my hawk or hound, but twenty times as much on my wife.”
“A hundred, then,” cried Lucentio, Bianca’s husband.
“Agreed,” cried the others.
Then Lucentio sent a message to the lovely Bianca, telling her to come to him. Baptista said he was sure his daughter would come. But the servant came back and said—
“Sir, my mistress is busy and cannot come.”
“There’s an answer for you,” said Petruchio.
“You may count yourself lucky if your wife doesn’t send you a worse one.”
“I hope a better one,” Petruchio answered. Then Hortensio said—
“Go and ask my wife to come to me at once.”
“Oh—if you have to ask her,” said Petruchio.
“I am afraid,” answered Hortensio sharply, “that whatever you do, yours won’t be asked.”
But now the servant came back in and said—
“She says you must be playing a joke, and she will not come.”
“Better and better,” cried Petruchio. “Now go back to your mistress and tell her I order her to come to me.”
They all burst out laughing, sure they knew her answer already: she would not come.
Then suddenly Baptista cried—
“Here comes Katharine!” And sure enough, there she was.
“What do you want, sir?” she asked her husband.
“Where are your sister and Hortensio’s wife?”
“Talking by the parlor fire.”
“Bring them here.”
When she had gone to fetch them, Lucentio said—
“This is a wonder!”
“I wonder what it means,” said Hortensio.
“It means peace,” said Petruchio, “and love, and a quiet life.”
“Well,” said Baptista, “the wager is yours, and I’ll add twenty thousand crowns more to her dowry, as though for a second daughter, because she is so changed that she seems like a different woman.”

So Petruchio won his wager, and he always had in Katharine a loving and faithful wife. Now that he had broken her proud, angry spirit, he loved her dearly, and there was never anything but love between the two of them. And so they lived happily ever after.

chapters.title: Measure for Measure
paragraphs: Longer ago than I care to say, the people of Vienna were ruled too gently. The reason was that their Duke, Vicentio, was far too good-natured and hated to see wrongdoers made unhappy.

As a result, the number of badly behaved people in Vienna grew until it was enough to make the Duke shake his head in sorrow when his chief secretary showed him the total at the bottom of a list. He decided, therefore, that wrongdoers must be punished. But he valued his popularity. He knew that if he suddenly turned strict after being easygoing, people would call him a tyrant. So he told his Privy Council that he had to go to Poland on important state business. “I have chosen Angelo to rule while I am away,” he said.

Now, this Angelo looked noble but was really a petty man. He had promised to marry a girl named Mariana, and then wanted nothing more to do with her once her dowry was lost. So poor Mariana lived in sadness, listening each day for the footstep of her stingy sweetheart, and loving him still.

Once he had appointed Angelo his deputy, the Duke went to a friar named Thomas and asked him for a friar’s robe and lessons in how to give religious counsel. He did not intend to go to Poland at all, but to stay at home and see how Angelo governed.
Angelo had not been a day in office when he condemned a young man named Claudio to death for an act of rash selfishness that today would earn nothing worse than a severe scolding.
Claudio had an odd friend named Lucio, and Lucio saw a way for Claudio to go free: if Claudio’s lovely sister Isabella would beg Angelo for mercy.
At that time Isabella was living in a convent. No man had won her heart, and she thought she would like to become a sister, which is to say a nun.
In the meantime Claudio had another person speaking up for him.
An elderly lord named Escalus argued for gentleness. “Let us cut a little, but not kill,” he said. “This young man had a very noble father.”
Angelo would not be moved. “If twelve jurors find me guilty, I ask for no more mercy than the law gives.”
Angelo then told the Provost to make sure Claudio was put to death at nine o’clock the next morning.
Soon after he gave this order, someone told Angelo that the condemned man’s sister wished to see him.
“Let her in,” said Angelo.
Isabella came in with Lucio. “I am a sorrowful petitioner to your Honor,” the lovely girl said.
“Well?” said Angelo.

His cold, one-word reply made her blush, and the rising color only made her face more beautiful. “I have a brother who has been condemned to die,” she went on. “Condemn the fault, I beg you, and spare my brother.”
“Every fault,” said Angelo, “is judged guilty before it is ever done. A fault itself cannot suffer. Justice would be empty if whoever committed a fault were allowed to walk away.”
She would have walked out of the court if Lucio had not whispered to her, “You are too cold. You could not plead more feebly if you were asking for a pin.”

So Isabella went at Angelo again. When he said, “I will not pardon him,” she was not discouraged, and when he said, “He is sentenced; it is too late,” she charged right back in. But she fought only with arguments, and with arguments alone she could not beat the Deputy.

She told him that nothing suits power so well as mercy. She told him that all people receive mercy from Heaven and need it, and that it is good to have a giant’s strength but wrong to use it like a giant. She told him that lightning splits the oak and spares the myrtle. She urged him to search his own heart for faults, and if he found one, not to use it as a reason to take her brother’s life.
At that very moment Angelo did find a fault in his heart. He loved Isabella’s beauty, and he was tempted to do for her beauty what he would never do out of kindness to anyone.
He seemed to give way a little, for he said, “Come to me tomorrow before noon.”
At any rate, she had won her brother a few more hours of life.
After she had gone, Angelo’s conscience scolded him for playing games with his duty as a judge.
When Isabella came to see him the second time, he told her, “Your brother cannot live.”
Isabella was shocked and hurt, but all she said was, “So be it. Heaven keep your Honor.”
But as she turned to leave, Angelo felt that his duty and his honor counted for little next to the thought of losing her.
“Give me your love,” he said, “and Claudio will be set free.”
“Before I would marry you, he should die, even if he had twenty heads to put on the block,” Isabella answered, for she now saw that Angelo was not the upright man he pretended to be.

Then she went to her brother in his cell to tell him he must die. At first he spoke boldly and promised to embrace the darkness of death. But when he understood that his sister could buy his life by marrying Angelo, he decided his life was worth more than her happiness, and he cried out, “Sweet sister, let me live.”
“You cowardly, faithless wretch! You dishonorable creature!” she cried.
Just then the Duke stepped forward, dressed as a friar, and asked to speak with Isabella. He called himself Friar Lodowick.

The Duke told her that Angelo was engaged to Mariana, and he related her love story. Then he asked her to consider a plan. Mariana would dress in Isabella’s clothes and go to Angelo closely veiled, and she would say, in a voice like Isabella’s, that if Claudio were spared she would marry him. She should take the ring from Angelo’s little finger, so that it could later be proved that his visitor had been Mariana.
Isabella naturally had great respect for friars, who are as close to nuns as men can get. So she agreed to the Duke’s plan. They would meet again at the moated grange, which was Mariana’s home.
Out in the street the Duke came across Lucio. Lucio saw a man in a friar’s habit and called to him, “Any word of the Duke, friar?” “None,” the Duke answered.

Lucio then told the Duke a few stories about Angelo, and after that one about the Duke himself. The Duke said it was false. This annoyed Lucio, who called the Duke “a shallow, ignorant fool,” even though he claimed to love him. “The Duke shall know you better, if I live to report you,” the Duke said grimly. Next he saw Escalus in the street and asked what he thought of his ruler. Escalus, believing he was talking to a friar, answered, “The Duke is a very moderate gentleman, who would rather watch someone else be merry than be merry himself.”
Then the Duke went to visit Mariana.

Isabella arrived right after him, and the Duke introduced the two young women to each other. Both of them believed he was a friar. They went into another room, away from him, to talk about saving Claudio. While they spoke in low, earnest voices, the Duke looked out the window and saw the broken sheds and the flower beds black with moss, which showed how little Mariana cared for her country home. Some women would have made the garden pretty, but not she. She preferred the town and ignored the pleasures of the country. He felt sure Angelo would not make her any unhappier than that.
“We are agreed, father,” said Isabella as she came back with Mariana.
And so Angelo was fooled by the girl he had cast out of his love, and he put on her finger a ring he wore, set with a milky stone that flashed in the light with hidden colors.

When he heard it had worked, the Duke went to the prison the next day, expecting to learn that an order had come for Claudio’s release. It had not. Instead, while he waited, a letter was handed to the Provost. The Duke was astonished when the Provost read these words aloud: “Whatever you may hear to the contrary, have Claudio executed by four o’clock. Send me his head by five.”

But the Duke said to the Provost, “You must show the Deputy another head.” He held out a letter and a signet. “Here,” he said, “are the handwriting and the seal of the Duke. I tell you, he is coming back, and Angelo does not know it. Give Angelo another head.”
The Provost thought, “This friar talks like a man with power behind him. That is the Duke’s own seal, and that is his own hand.”
At last he said, “A man died in the prison this morning, a pirate, the same age as Claudio, with a beard the same color. I will show his head.”
The pirate’s head was shown to Angelo in due course, and he was fooled by how much it looked like Claudio’s.

The Duke’s return was so welcome that the citizens lifted the city gates off their hinges to help him enter Vienna. Angelo and Escalus came forward to greet him and were warmly praised for how they had run things while the Duke was away.
That made it all the more uncomfortable for Angelo when Isabella, furious at his treachery, knelt before the Duke and cried out for justice.
When she had told her story, the Duke cried, “Take her to prison for slandering my right hand! But wait, who talked you into coming here?”
“Friar Lodowick,” she said.
“Who knows him?” asked the Duke.
“I do, my lord,” Lucio answered. “I gave him a beating for speaking ill of your Grace.”
A friar named Peter spoke up then: “Friar Lodowick is a holy man.”
An officer led Isabella away, and Mariana stepped forward. She took off her veil and said to Angelo, “This is the face you once swore was worth looking at.”
He faced her bravely as she held out her hand and said, “This is the hand that wears the ring you meant to give to someone else.”
“I do know this woman,” said Angelo. “Marriage was once discussed between us, but I decided she was shallow.”
Mariana burst out that they were engaged by the strongest vows. Angelo answered by asking the Duke to insist that Friar Lodowick be brought in.
“He shall appear,” the Duke promised. He told Escalus to question the missing witness thoroughly while he himself was away.

Soon the Duke came back as Friar Lodowick, with Isabella and the Provost beside him. Escalus did not so much question him as abuse and threaten him. Lucio told him to deny, if he dared, that he had called the Duke a fool and a coward and had his nose pulled for his insolence.
“Take him to prison!” shouted Escalus. But as the guards laid hands on him, the Duke pulled off his friar’s hood and stood before them all as the Duke.
“Now,” he said to Angelo, “if you have any boldness left that can still help you, make the most of it.”
“All I beg for is a quick sentence and death,” was the answer.
“Were you engaged to Mariana?” the Duke asked.
“I was,” said Angelo.
“Then marry her at once,” said his master. “Marry them,” he told Friar Peter, “and come back here with them.”

“Come here, Isabel,” the Duke said in a gentle voice. “Your friar is now your Prince, and he is sorry he was too late to save your brother.” But the mischievous Duke knew very well that he had saved him.
“Oh, forgive me,” she cried, “for making my Sovereign serve me in my trouble.”
“You are forgiven,” he said cheerfully.
Just then Angelo and his wife came back in. “And now, Angelo,” said the Duke gravely, “we sentence you to the block where Claudio laid his head!”
“Oh, my most gracious lord,” cried Mariana, “do not mock me!”
“You will be buying yourself a better husband,” said the Duke.
“Oh, my dear lord,” she said, “I ask for no better man.”
Isabella nobly joined her plea to Mariana’s, but the Duke pretended to be unbending.
“Provost,” he said, “why was Claudio put to death at such an odd hour?”
The Provost was afraid to admit the lie he had told Angelo, so he said, “I had a private message.”

“You are removed from your office,” said the Duke, and the Provost left. Angelo said, “I am sorry that I caused so much grief. I choose death over mercy.” Before long there was a stir in the crowd, and the Provost came back with Claudio. Like a great overgrown child, the Provost announced, “I saved this man; he looks like Claudio.” The Duke was amused. He told Isabella, “I forgive him because he looks like your brother. He looks like my brother too, if you, dear Isabel, will be mine.”
She became his with a smile, and the Duke forgave Angelo and gave the Provost a promotion.
Lucio he sentenced to marry a sturdy woman with a sharp tongue.

chapters.title: Two Gentlemen of Verona
paragraphs: Only one of them was truly a gentleman, as you will find out later. Their names were Valentine and Proteus. They were friends and lived in Verona, a town in northern Italy. Valentine was lucky in his name, since it belonged to the patron saint of lovers, and a Valentine finds it hard to be fickle or mean. Proteus was unlucky in his, since it belonged to a famous shape-changer, and that encouraged him to be a lover one moment and a traitor the next.
One day Valentine told his friend he was going to Milan. “I’m not in love the way you are,” he said, “so I have no wish to stay at home.”

Proteus was in love with a beautiful yellow-haired girl named Julia, who was rich and had nobody to boss her around. Still, he was sad to say goodbye to Valentine, and he said, “If you are ever in danger, let me know, and I will pray for you.” Valentine then set off for Milan with a servant named Speed, and in Milan he fell in love with Silvia, the Duke of Milan’s daughter.

When Proteus and Valentine parted, Julia had not admitted that she loved Proteus. In fact, she had torn up one of his letters in front of her maid, Lucetta. But Lucetta was no fool. When she saw the pieces she said to herself, “All she wants is to be annoyed by another letter.” And sure enough, as soon as Lucetta left her alone, Julia regretted tearing it up and tucked the scrap of paper with Proteus’s signature between her dress and her heart. So by tearing up a letter from Proteus, she found out that she loved him. Then, like a brave and sweet girl, she wrote to Proteus, “Be patient, and you shall marry me.”
Delighted by these words, Proteus strolled about waving Julia’s letter and talking to himself.
“What do you have there?” asked his father, Antonio.
“A letter from Valentine,” Proteus lied.
“Let me read it,” said Antonio.
“Nothing new,” said the sly Proteus. “He just says he is very happy, that the Duke of Milan treats him kindly, and that he wishes I could join him.”

This lie made Antonio think his son should go to Milan and enjoy the favors Valentine was basking in. “You must go tomorrow,” he ordered. Proteus was dismayed. “Give me time to get my things ready.” He was told, “Whatever you need will be sent after you.”

Julia was sad to part from her sweetheart when their engagement was not even two days old. She gave him a ring and said, “Keep this for my sake.” He gave her a ring in return, and they kissed like two people who mean to stay true until death. Then Proteus left for Milan.

Meanwhile Valentine was entertaining Silvia, whose gray eyes, laughing at him from under her auburn hair, had drowned him in love. One day she told him she wanted to write a pretty letter to a gentleman she thought well of but had no time. Would he write it for her? Valentine very much disliked writing that letter, but he wrote it and handed it to her coldly. “Take it back,” she said. “You wrote it unwillingly.”
“Madam,” he answered, “writing a letter like that for you was a hard thing to do.”
“Take it back,” she ordered. “You did not write it tenderly enough.”

Valentine was left holding the letter, with another to write. But his servant Speed saw what had really happened: Lady Silvia had got Valentine to write a love letter to Valentine himself. “The joke,” he said, “is as invisible as a weathercock on a steeple.” He meant it was very obvious, and he went on to say exactly what it was: “If master will write her love letters, he must answer them.”
When Proteus arrived, Valentine introduced him to Silvia. Later, when they were alone, Valentine asked Proteus how his love for Julia was going.
“Why,” said Proteus, “you used to get tired of hearing me talk about her.”
“I did,” Valentine confessed, “but now things are different. I can eat and drink the whole day long with only love on my plate and love in my cup.”
“You worship Silvia,” said Proteus.
“She is divine,” said Valentine.
“Come, come!” Proteus protested.
“Fine, perhaps she is not divine,” said Valentine, “but she is the queen of every woman on earth.”
“Except Julia,” said Proteus.
“My dear fellow,” said Valentine, “Julia is not left out; but I will grant that she alone is worthy to carry my lady’s train.”
“Your boasting amazes me,” said Proteus.

But Proteus had seen Silvia, and he suddenly felt that yellow-haired Julia looked black beside her. In his thoughts he instantly became a villain, and he said to himself what he had never said before—“I am dearer to myself than my friend.”

It would have been handy for Valentine if Proteus had used the power of the god he was named for and changed the shape of his body at that evil moment, when he turned his back on Julia by admiring Silvia. But his body did not change. His smile was as friendly as ever, and Valentine trusted him with the great secret that Silvia had now promised to run away with him. “In the pocket of this cloak,” said Valentine, “I have a rope ladder made of silk, with hooks that will catch on the bar of her window.”
Proteus understood why Silvia and her lover meant to run away. The Duke planned to marry her to Sir Thurio, a well-mannered fool whom she cared for not at all.

Proteus reasoned that if he could get Valentine out of the way, he might win Silvia’s affection for himself, especially if her father kept forcing Sir Thurio’s dull chatter on her. So he went to the Duke and said, “Duty comes before friendship! I am sorry to work against my friend Valentine, but your Grace ought to know that he plans to elope with your daughter tonight.” He asked the Duke not to let Valentine learn who had given him this news, and the Duke promised that his name would be kept secret.
Early that evening the Duke called Valentine to him, and Valentine arrived wearing a large cloak with a bulging pocket.
“You know,” said the Duke, “that I want my daughter to marry Sir Thurio?”
“I do,” answered Valentine. “He is virtuous and generous, which suits a man your Grace thinks so highly of.”
“Even so, she dislikes him,” said the Duke. “She is a sulky, proud, disobedient girl, and I would hate to leave her a penny. So I have decided to marry again myself.”
Valentine bowed.
“I hardly know how young people court each other these days,” the Duke went on, “and I thought you were exactly the man to teach me how to win the lady I have chosen.”
“Jewels have been known to speak up quite well,” said Valentine.
“I have tried them,” said the Duke.
“She may get into the habit of liking the giver, if your Grace sends her a few more.”
“The main trouble,” the Duke continued, “is this. The lady is promised to a young gentleman, and it is hard to get a word with her. In fact, she is kept locked up.”
“In that case, your Grace should propose running away together,” said Valentine. “A rope ladder would do it.”
“But how would I carry it?” asked the Duke.
“A rope ladder weighs very little,” said Valentine. “You can carry it in a cloak.”
“A cloak like yours?”
“Yes, your Grace.”
“Then yours will do. Please lend it to me.”

Valentine had talked himself into a trap. He could not refuse to lend his cloak, and once the Duke had put it on, his Grace pulled a sealed letter addressed to Silvia out of the pocket. He calmly opened it and read the words: “Silvia, you shall be free tonight.”
“So,” he said, “and here is the rope ladder. Cleverly planned, but not cleverly enough. Sir, I give you one day to leave my lands. If you are still in Milan at this time tomorrow, you die.”
Poor Valentine was crushed. “If I cannot see Silvia in daylight,” he said, “then there is no daylight for me to see.”
Before leaving, he said good-bye to Proteus, who turned out to be a first-class hypocrite. “Hope is a lover’s walking stick,” said the man who had betrayed him. “Go on your way with that.”

After leaving Milan, Valentine and his servant wandered into a forest near Mantua, where the great poet Virgil had lived. In that forest, though, the poets (if there were any) turned out to be bandits, who ordered the travelers to halt. They did, and Valentine made such a good impression on his captors that they offered to spare his life if he would become their captain.
“I accept,” said Valentine, “if you free my servant and never harm women or the poor.”
That was an answer worthy of Virgil, and Valentine became the chief of the bandits.

Now we go back to Julia, who found Verona much too dull to live in after Proteus left. She begged her maid Lucetta to think of some way she could see him. “You had better wait for him to come back,” said Lucetta, and she spoke so sensibly that Julia saw it was pointless to hope Lucetta would take the blame for any rash and exciting adventure. So Julia announced that she meant to go to Milan, dressed as a page.
“Then you will have to cut off your hair,” said Lucetta, who thought this news would make Julia drop her plan at once.
“I shall knot it up,” came the disappointing reply.

Lucetta then tried to make the plan look silly to Julia, but Julia had made up her mind and would not be laughed out of it. When she had finished dressing, she made as handsome a page as anyone could wish to see.
Julia took the boy’s name Sebastian, and reached Milan just as music was being played outside the Duke’s palace.
“They are serenading the Lady Silvia,” a man told her.
All at once a voice rose in song, and she knew it well. It was Proteus. But what was he singing?

“Who is Silvia? What is she,
That every shepherd praises her?
She is holy, fair, and wise;
Heaven gave her such grace
That she might be admired.”
Julia tried not to listen to the rest, but somehow these two lines rang in her mind like thunder—

“So let us sing to Silvia;
She surpasses every mortal thing.”

So Proteus thought Silvia surpassed Julia. And since he sang so beautifully for the whole world to hear, it seemed he was not just unfaithful to Julia but had forgotten her. Still, Julia loved him. She even went to him and asked to be his page, and Proteus took her on.
One day he gave her the ring she had once given him, and said, “Sebastian, take this to the Lady Silvia, and tell her I would like the picture of herself that she promised me.”

Silvia had promised the picture, but she disliked Proteus. She had to talk to him because he stood high in her father’s favor, and her father believed Proteus was pleading with her on behalf of Sir Thurio. Silvia had learned from Valentine that Proteus was promised to a sweetheart in Verona, and when he spoke tender words to her, she felt he was false in friendship as well as in love.
Julia brought the ring to Silvia, who refused it: “I will not wrong the woman who gave it to him by keeping it on my own hand.”
“She thanks you,” said Julia.
“Then you know her?” said Silvia, and Julia spoke so lovingly about herself that Silvia wished Sebastian would marry Julia.
Silvia gave Julia her portrait for Proteus. He would have received it looking worse, with a few extra touches added to the nose and eyes, if Julia had not decided that she was as pretty as Silvia.
Before long the palace was in an uproar. Silvia had run away.
The Duke felt sure she meant to join the banished Valentine, and he was right.
He set off after her at once, taking Sir Thurio, Proteus, and some servants.

The chasing party became scattered, and Proteus and Julia (still in her page’s clothes) were alone together when they saw Silvia, who had been captured by outlaws and was being taken to their Captain. Proteus rescued her, and then said, “I have saved you from death. Give me one kind look in return.”
“Oh, what misery, to owe my rescue to you!” cried Silvia. “I would sooner be eaten by a lion for breakfast.”
Julia stayed silent but cheerful. Proteus was so angry with Silvia that he threatened her and grabbed her by the waist.
“Oh, heaven!” cried Silvia.

At that moment came the sound of snapping branches. Valentine was crashing through the forest of Mantua to rescue the woman he loved. Julia feared he would kill Proteus and hurried to protect her unfaithful lover. But Valentine struck no blow. He only said, “Proteus, I am sorry that I can never trust you again.”
At that, Proteus felt his guilt, fell to his knees, and said, “Forgive me! I am sorry! I am suffering!”
“Then you are my friend again,” said generous Valentine. “If Silvia, whom I have lost, will look kindly on you, I promise to step aside and bless you both.”
These words were terrible to Julia, and she fainted. Valentine brought her around and asked, “What was the matter, boy?”
“I remembered,” Julia fibbed, “that I was told to give a ring to the Lady Silvia, and I never did.”
“Well, give it to me,” said Proteus.
She gave him a ring, but it was the one Proteus himself had given to Julia before leaving Verona.
Proteus stared at her hand and blushed crimson right up to his hair.
“I changed my shape when you changed your mind,” she said.
“But I love you again,” he said.
Just then some outlaws came in, bringing two prizes: the Duke and Sir Thurio.
“Stop!” cried Valentine sternly. “The Duke is not to be touched.”
Sir Thurio exclaimed, “There is Silvia, and she is mine!”
“Lay a hand on her and you die!” said Valentine.
“I would be foolish to risk my neck for her,” said Sir Thurio.
“Then you are a coward,” said the Duke. “Valentine, you are a brave man. Your banishment is over, and I call you back. You may marry Silvia. You have earned her.”
“I thank your Grace,” said Valentine, deeply moved, “but I must ask one more favor.”
“It is granted,” said the Duke.
“Forgive these men, your Grace, and give them work. They are better than the life they lead.”
“I forgive them, and you,” said the Duke. “From now on they will work for wages.”
“What does your Grace think of this page?” Valentine asked, pointing to Julia.
The Duke looked her over and said, “That boy has something graceful about him.”

“More grace than boy, I say,” laughed Valentine. And the only punishment Proteus had to endure for his betrayals of love and friendship was to sit and hear the adventures of Julia-Sebastian of Verona told in front of him.

chapters.title: All’s Well That Ends Well
paragraphs: Some time in the thirteen hundreds, the Countess of Rousillon sat sadly in her palace near the Pyrenees. Her husband was dead, and the King of France had sent for her son Bertram to come to Paris, hundreds of miles off.

Bertram was a handsome young man with curling hair, finely arched eyebrows, and eyes as sharp as a hawk’s. He was as proud as ignorance could make him, and he would lie with a face as honest as truth itself to get what he selfishly wanted. But a handsome youth is a handsome youth, and Helena was in love with him.
Helena was the daughter of a great doctor who had died serving the Count of Rousillon. Her whole fortune was a handful of her father’s prescriptions.

After Bertram left, the Countess noticed Helena’s sad face and told her she was exactly the same to her as her own child. Tears then filled Helena’s eyes, because she felt that the Countess’s words made Bertram seem like a brother, someone she could never marry. The Countess guessed her secret at once, and Helena confessed that Bertram was to her what the sun is to the day.

She hoped, though, to win this sun by earning the gratitude of the King of France, who had a lingering illness that left him lame. The great doctors of the Court had given up hope of curing him, but Helena trusted a prescription her father had used successfully.
She said an affectionate good-bye to the Countess, went to Paris, and was allowed to see the King.
He was very courteous, but plainly thought she was a fraud. “It would hardly be proper,” he said, “to ask a simple girl for the cure that all the learned doctors have failed to give me.”
“Heaven sometimes uses weak tools,” said Helena, and she declared she would give up her life if she failed to cure him.
“And if you succeed?” asked the King.
“Then I will ask your Majesty to let me have the man I choose as my husband!”
A suffering king could not hold out forever against so earnest a young woman. So Helena became the King’s doctor, and in two days the lame king could skip.

He called his courtiers, and they filled the throne room of his palace in a glittering crowd. The country girl might easily have been dazzled and spotted a dozen husbands worth dreaming of among the handsome young noblemen standing there. But her eyes simply roamed until they landed on Bertram. She walked up to him and said, “I dare not say I take you, but I am yours!” Then she raised her voice so the King would hear, and added, “This is the Man!”
“Bertram,” said the King, “take her. She is your wife!”
“My wife, my lord?” said Bertram. “I beg your Majesty to let me choose my own wife.”
“Bertram, do you understand what she has done for your King?” asked the monarch, who had always treated him like a son.
“I do, your Majesty,” Bertram replied, “but why should I marry a girl who was raised on my father’s charity?”

“You look down on her because she has no title, but I can give her one,” said the King. As he looked at the sulky young man, a thought struck him, and he added, “It is strange that you think so much of blood, when you could not tell your own from a beggar’s if you saw them mixed together in a bowl.”
“I cannot love her,” insisted Bertram. Helena said gently, “Do not press him, your Majesty. I am glad to have cured my King, for my country’s sake.”

“My honor demands obedience from that scornful boy,” said the King. “Bertram, make up your mind to this. Either you marry this lady, whom you do not deserve, or you will learn how a king can hate. What is your answer?”
Bertram bowed low and said, “Your Majesty has raised the lady to nobility by taking such an interest in her. I submit.”
“Take her hand,” said the King, “and say that she is yours.”
Bertram did so, and soon afterward he was married to Helena.

But fear of the King could not turn him into a loving husband. Mockery made him bitter too. A low soldier named Parolles told him to his face that now that he had a “kicky-wicky,” his business was not to fight but to stay at home. “Kicky-wicky” was only a silly name for a wife, but it made Bertram feel he could not stand having a wife, and that he must go to the war in Italy, even though the King had forbidden it.
He ordered Helena to say good-bye to the King and go back to Rousillon, and he gave her letters for his mother and for herself. Then he rode away, saying a cold farewell.
She opened the letter meant for her and read: “When you can get the ring off my finger, you may call me your husband. But next to that ‘when,’ I write ‘never.’”

Helena had kept her eyes dry when she came before the King and said farewell, but he was worried about her, and he gave her a ring from his own finger, saying, “If you send me this, I will know you are in trouble, and I will help you.”

She kept Bertram’s letter to his wife from the King, since it would have made him want to kill the runaway Count. Instead she returned to Rousillon and gave her mother-in-law the other letter. It was short and bitter. “I have run away,” it said. “If the world is big enough, I will stay far away from her always.”
“Take heart,” the noble widow told the wife he had left behind. “I wash his name out of my blood. You are my only child now.”
The Dowager Countess was still enough of a mother to Bertram, however, to blame his behavior on Parolles, whom she called “a very tainted fellow.”
Helena did not remain long at Rousillon. She put on a pilgrim’s dress, left a letter for her mother-in-law, and slipped away toward Florence.
When she entered that city, she asked a woman the way to the Pilgrims’ House of Rest, but the woman urged “the holy pilgrim” to stay at her own home.
Helena learned that her hostess was a widow whose daughter, Diana, was very beautiful.

When Diana heard that Helena came from France, she said, “A countryman of yours, Count Rousillon, has done fine service for Florence.” But after a while Diana had something to tell that did Helena’s husband no credit at all. Bertram was courting Diana. He did not hide that he was married, but Diana had heard from Parolles that his wife was not worth caring about.
The widow worried about Diana, and Helena made up her mind to tell her who she really was, the Countess Rousillon.
“He keeps begging Diana for a lock of her hair,” the widow said.

Helena smiled sadly, because her own hair was as fine as Diana’s and exactly the same color. Then a thought came to her, and she said, “Please keep this purse of gold. I will give Diana three thousand crowns if she helps me carry out a plan. She must promise my husband a lock of her hair, if he will hand over the ring he wears on his finger. It has been in his family for generations, and five Counts of Rousillon have worn it, yet he will give it away in exchange for a lock of your daughter’s hair. Have her insist that he cut the lock in a dark room, and agree beforehand that she shall not say one word.”
The widow heard her out with the purse of gold resting in her lap. At last she said, “I agree, if Diana is willing.”

Diana was willing. Oddly enough, Bertram liked the idea of cutting a lock of hair from a silent girl in a dark room so much that he gave Diana his ring, and she told him when to come to her. At the appointed hour he arrived with a sharp knife. As he cut the lock he felt a soft cheek brush his own, and he left the room well pleased with himself, like a man covered in glory. On his finger was a ring that the girl in the dark room had given him.

The war was almost over, but one of its last episodes showed Bertram that the soldier who had dared to call Helena his “kicky-wicky” had much less courage than a wife. Parolles was such a braggart, and so vain about the frills on his clothes, that the French officers set a trap to find out what he was really made of. He had lost his drum, and he had announced that he would win it back or die trying. His effort was feeble, and he was busy making up a story of a heroic failure when he was surrounded and disarmed.
“Portotartarossa,” said one of the French lords.
“What terrible gibberish is that?” thought Parolles, who had a blindfold over his eyes.
“He is calling for the torturers,” said a Frenchman, pretending to be an interpreter. “What will you tell us if we do without them?”

“Just as much,” answered Parolles, “as I could possibly tell you if you squeezed me like a pie crust.” He kept his word. He told them how many men served in each regiment of the Florentine army, and he treated them to juicy stories about the officers who commanded it.
Bertram was there too, and he listened as a letter was read aloud in which Parolles told Diana that Bertram was a fool.
“There is your devoted friend,” said a French lord.
“To me he is a cat now,” said Bertram, who hated hearth pets.
In the end Parolles was set free, but from then on he went about feeling like a sneak, and he gave up boasting.

Now we go back to France with Helena. She had let a rumor spread that she was dead, and the news was carried to the Dowager Countess at Rousillon by Lafeu, a lord who hoped to marry his daughter Magdalen to Bertram.
The King grieved for Helena, but he approved the match planned for Bertram, and he traveled to Rousillon to see it carried out.
“His great offense is dead and buried,” he said. “Let Bertram come to me.”

Bertram came forward with a scar on his cheek and knelt before his Sovereign. He said that if he had not loved Lafeu’s daughter before he married Helena, he would have valued the wife he loved now, too late.
“Love that comes late offends Heaven,” said the King. “Forget sweet Helena, and give Magdalen a ring.”
Bertram at once handed a ring to Lafeu, who cried out angrily, “That is Helena’s!”
“It is not!” said Bertram.

At this the King asked to see the ring and said, “This is the ring I gave Helena. I told her to send it back to me if she ever needed help. So you were sly enough to take from her the very thing that could have helped her most.”
Again Bertram insisted the ring had never been Helena’s, yet his own mother declared that it had.

“You are lying!” cried the King. “Guards, seize him!” Yet even as the guards took hold of him, Bertram was puzzling over how the ring he believed Diana had given him could look so much like Helena’s. Just then a gentleman came in and asked leave to give the King a petition. It was signed Diana Capilet, and it begged the King to order Bertram to marry the girl he had abandoned after winning her love.
“I would rather buy a son-in-law at a fair than accept Bertram now,” said Lafeu.
“Bring in the petitioner,” said the King.

Bertram suddenly found himself face to face with Diana and her mother. He denied that Diana had any claim on him, and he talked about her as if she had spent her life in the gutter. But she asked what kind of gentlewoman it could be to whom he had given, as he had given to her, the ring of his ancestors, which was now missing from his finger.
Bertram wished the ground would swallow him, but fate still had one final kindness in store for him. Helena walked in.
“Am I seeing what is real?” asked the King.
“Oh, forgive me! Forgive me!” cried Bertram.
She held up his family ring. “Now that this is mine,” she said, “will you love me, Bertram?”
“As long as I live,” he cried.
“My eyes smell onions,” said Lafeu, as tears for Helena sparkled in them.

When the young lady, who was not at all shy, had explained her conduct fully, the King praised Diana. For Helena’s sake she had wanted to show up Bertram’s meanness, not only to the King but to Bertram himself. His pride now hung in tatters, and people believe that he did turn out to be a husband of some kind after all.
